1removedimport TS.SFLCompat

3removed-- # Typeclasses
4removed
5removed-- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6removed-- variable with no constraint on it:
7removed
8removedvariable (α : Type)
9removed
10removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11removed-- Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
12removed-- lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13removed--
14removed-- `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15removed--
16removed-- Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?
17removed
18removed-- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
19removed-- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
20removed-- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
21removed-- `a : α`.
22removed
23removed-- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
24removed-- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
25removed-- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
26removed-- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
27removed-- languages, such as traits in Rust.
28removed
29removed-- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
30removed
31removed-- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
32removed-- occurs in a list:
33removed
34removeddef List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
35removed match xs with
36removed | [] => false
37removed | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
38removed
39removedtheorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
40removed
41removedtheorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
42removed (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
43removed
44removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
45removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
46removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
47removed
48removed-- What if we want this to work for lists of **any** element type, not just
49removed-- `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a type
50removed-- variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
51removed
52removed-- Note to developers:
53removed-- @dsainati - The Verso compilation is not actually removing this from
54removed-- the generated file despite th e -keep flag. It is, however, stripping
55removed-- the message guard, so this results in an error. Once we figure out how
56removed-- we are handling these cases, uncomment this.
57removed--
58removed-- `/--
59removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
60removed-- BEq α
61removed--
62removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
63removed-- -/
64removed-- #guard_msgs in
65removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
66removed-- match xs with
67removed-- | [] => false
68removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
69removed--
70removed-- `/--
71removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
72removed-- BEq α
73removed--
74removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
75removed-- -/
76removed-- #guard_msgs in
77removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
78removed-- match xs with
79removed-- | [] => false
80removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
81removed--
82removed-- `/--
83removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
84removed-- BEq α
85removed--
86removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
87removed-- -/
88removed-- #guard_msgs in
89removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
90removed-- match xs with
91removed-- | [] => false
92removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
93removed
94removed-- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on a
95removed-- value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one way
96removed-- to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test to use.
97removed
98removedsf_experiment
99removed def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
100removed match xs with
101removed | [] => false
102removed | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
103removed
104removed #eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
105removed
106removed-- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
107removed-- supply, the right equality function.
108removed
109removed-- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
110removed-- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify
111removed-- something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the needed
112removed-- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
113removed-- Rust. Particular *implementations* of that interface, different ones for
114removed-- different types, are called *instances*. Finally, we add the name of that
115removed-- class as a *typeclass constraint* on the polymorphic variable that the
116removed-- function applies to. This directs Lean to use the interface inside the
117removed-- function, and to find and fill in the appropriate instance at call-sites to
118removed-- that function. Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
119removed
120removeddef List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
121removed match xs with
122removed | [] => false
123removed | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
124removed
125removedtheorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
126removed
127removedtheorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
128removed (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
129removed
130removed#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
131removed
132removed-- As Lists noted when we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq`
133removed-- typeclass, and it's what `List.elem_poly` uses internally wherever it
134removed-- writes `==`. This is done using **instance implicits**, where we place a
135removed-- desired typeclass assumption in square bracket. The `[BEq α]` constraint is
136removed-- saying that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at call sites for the
137removed-- *particular* type `α` that is used. In the example `[0, 1].elem_poly 0`,
138removed-- this type is `Nat`, and the automatically chosen instance corresponds to
139removed-- `Nat.beq`.
140removed
141removed-- Note to developers (xhalo32):
142removed-- This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes from
143removed-- `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of
144removed-- `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
145removed-- how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
146removed
147removed-- In the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, `α` was fully generic, with no
148removed-- typeclass constraint — so the `==` in its body would have needed to work
149removed-- for *every* type `α`, and no single `BEq` instance can do that. That's why
150removed-- Lean's search failed.
151removed
152removed-- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far. We'll
153removed-- see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how to define
154removed-- a typeclass in the first place.
155removed
156removed-- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
157removed
158removed-- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of our
159removed-- own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis — that made
160removed-- `==` resolve automatically above.
161removed
162removed-- Suppose we want to specify that a type has at least one inhabitant, i.e.,
163removed-- that it is not empty. A `structure` (chapter Lists) can express this
164removed-- directly:
165removed
166removedstructure HasOneStruct (α : Type) where
167removed one : α
168removed
169removed-- A value of `HasOneStruct Nat` witnesses that `Nat` is inhabited: it's built
170removed-- the same way any structure is, by supplying a `Nat` for the `one` field:
171removed
172removeddef nat_hasOneStruct : HasOneStruct Nat where
173removed one := 1
174removed
175removedexample : nat_hasOneStruct.one = 1 := rfl
176removed
177removed-- But nothing makes Lean produce this witness **automatically**: we had to
178removed-- write `⟨1⟩` ourselves, unlike the `BEq Nat` instance that Lean found for us
179removed-- on its own above.
180removed
181removed-- Typeclasses solve this. In Lean, they're implemented as structures and
182removed-- declared the same way, but with `class` in place of `structure`:
183removed
184removedclass HasOne (α : Type) where
185removed one : α
186removed
187removed-- The difference is in how we provide values of this type. Instead of `def`,
188removed-- we use `instance`:
189removed
190removed-- Note to developers:
191removed-- From GitHub (@chenson2018): Part of the point here is that we don't
192removed-- usually refer to instances explicitly, even me providing an explicit
193removed-- name is for pedagogy reasons. I'll make it more explicit in the text
194removed-- that what we're looking for in the infoview is the presence of this
195removed-- instance.
196removed
197removedinstance instHasOneNat : HasOne Nat where
198removed one := 1
199removed
200removed-- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via **typeclass synthesis** (or
201removed-- **typeclass inference**) — the same process that found `BEq Nat` earlier.
202removed-- To see it choose between instances, declare a second one, for `Int`, the
203removed-- type of integers `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
204removed
205removedinstance instHasOneInt : HasOne Int where
206removed one := -1
207removed
208removed-- Now `HasOne.one` alone, with no instance named, is enough — Lean infers
209removed-- which instance we mean from the expected type:
210removed
211removedexample : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
212removedexample : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
213removed
214removed-- These are the same as naming the instances explicitly:
215removed
216removedexample : instHasOneNat.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
217removedexample : instHasOneInt.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
218removed
219removed-- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
220removed
221removedset_option pp.all true in
222removedexample : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
223removed
224removedset_option pp.all true in
225removedexample : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
226removed
227removed-- which reveals `@HasOne.one Nat instHasOneNat` and
228removed-- `@HasOne.one Int instHasOneInt` on the right-hand side of each equality.
229removed-- The `#synth` command runs the same search directly:
230removed
231removed#synth HasOne Nat
232removed
233removed-- instHasOneNat
234removed
235removed-- For a typeclass like `HasOne` that carries data — a term, such as the `1`
236removed-- above, rather than only proofs — we expect at most one instance per type,
237removed-- so this search has a unique answer.
238removed
239removed-- Note to developers:
240removed-- @chenson2018: I don't really want to explain diamonds here, is the
241removed-- above white lie hand-waving okay??
242removed
243removed-- We'll put `HasOne`'s standard-library cousin, `Inhabited`, to work later in
244removed-- this chapter, when maps need a default value for a generic type. First,
245removed-- though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and see how its `[BEq α]`
246removed-- argument actually gets resolved.
247removed
248removed-- ## Using Typeclasses
249removed
250removed-- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
251removed-- turned off:
252removed
253removedset_option pp.notation false in
254removed#check 1 == 2
255removed
256removed-- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a field
257removed-- of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
258removed
259removed-- class BEq (α : Type u) where
260removed-- /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
261removed-- beq : α → α → Bool
262removed
263removed-- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
264removed-- type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `HasOne` instance
265removed-- above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
266removed
267removedinstance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
268removed beq := Nat.beq
269removed
270removed-- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly` is
271removed-- called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing `instHasOneNat`
272removed-- for `HasOne.one` earlier.
273removed
274removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
275removed
276removed-- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when specialized to
277removed-- natural numbers.
278removed
279removedtheorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
280removed sorry
281removed
282removed-- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
283removed
284removed-- Notably, the above examples enforce no conditions on the data that they
285removed-- carry, and we could provide any value that we would like for `HasOne.one`.
286removed-- This could be misleading, for instance if we had instead defined an
287removed-- instance
288removed
289removedsf_experiment
290removed instance : HasOne Nat where
291removed one := 2
292removed
293removed-- we might have some counterintuitive proofs based on the name leading us to
294removed-- believe the class contained the element `1`. In most languages that support
295removed-- typeclasses it is not possible to enforce a notion of "lawfulness" as part
296removed-- of the typeclass, and it falls to the author to ensure that any desired
297removed-- invariants are satisfied.
298removed
299removed-- As an example, suppose that we wanted to express the idea that a type has
300removed-- at least two distinct elements. A first attempt might be
301removed
302removedsf_experiment
303removed class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
304removed one : α
305removed two : α
306removed
307removed-- but this does not disallow the case where `one` and `two` are equal. In a
308removed-- proof assistant, however, typeclasses can also carry proofs along with
309removed-- data, so we can write
310removed
311removedclass HasTwo (α : Type) where
312removed one : α
313removed two : α
314removed one_neq_two : one ≠ two
315removed
316removed-- to enforce that these are two distinct entries. Declaring instances works
317removed-- in much the same way as before, except that now `HasTwo.one_neq_two`
318removed-- requires a proof:
319removed
320removedinstance : HasTwo Nat where
321removed one := 1
322removed two := 2
323removed one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
324removed
325removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
326removed
327removed-- Following the pattern of `HasOne` and `HasTwo`, define a class `HasThree`
328removed-- that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements.
329removed
330removed-- Note to developers (Claude, NOW):
331removed-- Rendering bug in this exercise and `instHasThree` below. Both use the
332removed-- `-- SOLUTION`/`-- END SOLUTION` comment-marker idiom to hide **some**
333removed-- class fields / instance fields, but the Verso HTML build does not
334removed-- process those markers (only the `solution!` tactic is handled). In
335removed-- **student** and **terse** the class shows only the visible fields while
336removed-- the `instHasThree` instance then reports a spurious
337removed-- `Fields missing: one_neq_three, two_neq_three` error; in **solutions**
338removed-- the hidden fields are shown but the literal `-- SOLUTION` /
339removed-- `-- END SOLUTION` comment lines leak into the displayed code. The
340removed-- generated `.lean` is fine — HTML-only. Fix by expressing the hidden
341removed-- fields with `solution!` rather than the comment markers.
342removed
343removedclass HasThree (α : Type) where
344removed one : α
345removed two : α
346removed three : α
347removed one_neq_two : one ≠ two
348removed -- FILL IN HERE
349removed
350removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): instHasThree ⭐
351removed
352removed-- Provide an instance of `HasThree` for `Nat`.
353removed
354removedinstance : HasThree Nat where
355removed one := 1
356removed two := 2
357removed three := 3
358removed one_neq_two := sorry
359removed -- FILL IN HERE
360removed
361removed-- ## Maps
362removed
363removed-- Maps (or dictionaries) are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
364removed-- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
365removed-- them in many places in the coming chapters.
366removed
367removed-- We'll define two flavors of maps: total maps, which include a "default"
368removed-- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
369removed-- partial maps, which instead return an option to indicate success or
370removed-- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as
371removed-- the default element.
372removed
373removed-- ### Identifiers
374removed
375removed-- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
376removed-- into our maps. Instead of using concrete types, we will use a type
377removed-- variables
378removed
379removedvariable {α : Type} {β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
380removed
381removedset_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
382removed
383removed-- where `α` is the type of our map keys and `β` the corresponding values.
384removed-- Looking at `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`, we see that these typeclasses:
385removed
386removed-- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
387removed-- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
388removed-- /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
389removed-- protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
390removed
391removed-- /--
392removed-- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
393removed
394removed-- In other words:
395removed-- * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
396removed-- * `a == a` is true.
397removed-- -/
398removed-- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
399removed-- /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
400removed-- eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
401removed
402removed-- provide the assumption that we have an boolean equality (`==`) on our keys
403removed-- that is reflexive and coincides with proposition equality `=`.
404removed
405removed-- ### Total Maps
406removed
407removed-- Our main job in this chapter will be to build a definition of partial maps
408removed-- that is similar in behavior to the one we saw in the Lists chapter, plus
409removed-- accompanying lemmas about its behavior.
410removed
411removed-- This time around, though, we're going to use functions, rather than lists
412removed-- of key-value pairs, to build maps. The advantage of this representation is
413removed-- that it offers a more "extensional" view of maps: two maps that respond to
414removed-- queries in the same way will be represented as exactly the same function,
415removed-- rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs
416removed-- that use maps.
417removed
418removed-- We build up to partial maps in two steps. First, we define total maps that
419removed-- return a default value when we look up a key that is not present in the
420removed-- map.
421removed
422removeddef TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := α → β
423removed
424removednamespace TotalMap
425removed
426removed-- Intuitively, a total map over an element type `β` is just a function that
427removed-- can be looked up using a corresponding `a : α`.
428removed
429removed-- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
430removed-- typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our `HasOne`
431removed-- example from above:
432removed
433removedvariable [Inhabited β]
434removed
435removed-- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a default
436removed-- element; this map always returns the default element when applied to any
437removed-- string.
438removed
439removeddef empty : TotalMap α β := fun _ ↦ default
440removed
441removed-- and we'll also declare an instance
442removed
443removedinstance : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
444removed emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
445removed
446removed-- so that we can use the `∅` notation for this empty map.
447removed
448removed-- #### Getting Elements
449removed
450removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
451removed-- This introductory bit seems heavier than necessary. Why not just say
452removed-- that we want to treat TotalMap as an abstract thing, not rely on the
453removed-- fact that it is defined in terms of functions, and then go ahead and do
454removed-- that?
455removed
456removed-- To access values in a map (i.e., a function), we can apply the map to a
457removed-- key:
458removed
459removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson (chenson2018), Niklas Halonen (xhalo32)):
460removed-- Using `default` in the early examples might be confusing. We could use
461removed-- something concrete, like `0` which is the default `Nat` instead.
462removed
463removedexample : (∅ : TotalMap Nat Nat) 1 = default := rfl
464removed
465removedend TotalMap
466removed
467removed-- Here we have made use of the the fact that the type `TotalMap` is defined
468removed-- as a function type, so technically Lean lets us use a function application
469removed-- to get an element. While this is possible, it goes against the spirit we
470removed-- have seen in previous chapters of defining interfaces to our types, like
471removed-- characterizing lemmas. We would like that the public interface we design
472removed-- for TotalMap to be independent of the fact that the definition is `α → β`.
473removed
474removed-- In the ideal, we should be able to substitute a different type with similar
475removed-- behavior without needing to change the public interface. Suppose, just for
476removed-- the sake of argument, that we wanted to define total maps as `List (α × β)`
477removed-- or `Std.HashMap α β`. Neither of these are functions, so the syntax `∅ 1`
478removed-- wouldn't work. If this is the public interface to access elements, it
479removed-- restricts the definition ot `TotalMap`, forcing it to be a function of some
480removed-- kind.
481removed
482removed-- To abstract away the function application, we introduce notation for
483removed-- accessing elements using square brackets. This let's us write `∅[1]` or
484removed-- `m[a]` regardless of the underlying definition of `TotalMap`.
485removed
486removed-- We'll call the typeclass `MyGetElem`. The typeclass takes three type
487removed-- parameters: the collection, the keys that can be used to index and the
488removed-- elements that it returns. For example, let's say we have declared an
489removed-- instance `MyGetElem (List Bool) Nat Bool`. One can think of the instance as
490removed-- saying that *indexing into `xs : List Bool` with an index `i : Nat` returns
491removed-- a `Bool`*. The notation we introduce for this is:
492removed-- `xs[i] = MyGetElem.getElem xs i`.
493removed
494removed-- Don't worry about what `outParam Type` means (it's like a normal type
495removed-- parameter with a hint to Lean that helps typeclass inference). The
496removed-- `macro_rules` and the `app_unexpander` are minor technicalities for getting
497removed-- the syntax to work.
498removed
499removedclass MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
500removed getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
501removed
502removednamespace MyGetElem
503removedscoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => `(getElem $xs $i)
504removed
505removed@[app_unexpander getElem]
506removeddef unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
507removed | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
508removed | _ => throw ()
509removedend MyGetElem
510removed
511removedopen scoped MyGetElem
512removed
513removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
514removed-- Make sure we've really explained `open scoped` somewhere...
515removed
516removed-- To use the notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`, we add a
517removed-- `MyGetElem` instance for total maps.
518removed
519removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
520removed-- Have we explained `variable [Inhabited β]`?
521removed
522removednamespace TotalMap
523removedvariable [Inhabited β]
524removed
525removedinstance : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
526removed getElem m a := m a
527removed
528removedtheorem getElem_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m a := by rfl
529removed
530removedexample : (∅ : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = default := by rfl
531removed
532removed-- When proving some of the characterizing lemmas below, we will rewrite using
533removed-- `getElem_def`. However, `getElem_def` exposes the underlying implementation
534removed-- that accessing elements in total maps is a function application, therefore
535removed-- it should only be used sparingly, and only inside the `TotalMap` namespace.
536removed
537removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
538removed-- That is a bit mysterious.
539removed
540removed-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
541removed-- As per the discussion in
542removed-- `https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean/pull/166#discussion_r3690573597`,
543removed-- we should provide the reverse of `getElem_def` as a simp-lemma, but it
544removed-- doesn't seem to behave nicely:
545removed--
546removed-- `@[simp]
547removed-- theorem apply_eq_getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by rfl`
548removed--
549removed-- The reverse direction of `getElem_def` is provided as a `simp`-lemma.
550removed--
551removed-- `example (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by
552removed-- -- simp -- doesn't work (infinite loop)
553removed-- -- dsimp -- doesn't work (nothing happens)
554removed-- -- rw [apply_eq_getElem] -- doesn't work: The pattern to be substituted is a metavariable (`?m ?a`) in this equality: ?m ?a = ?m[?a]
555removed-- rw [apply_eq_getElem m a] -- works`
556removed--
557removed-- Explanation of the infinite loop by Yipeng Liu (berberman): To see why,
558removed-- with `trace.Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite` enabled and specifying maxSteps
559removed-- to simp, we can track what's going on:
560removed--
561removed-- `[Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
562removed-- m a
563removed-- ==>
564removed-- m[a]
565removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
566removed-- m[a]
567removed-- ==>
568removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
569removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
570removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
571removed-- ==>
572removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
573removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
574removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
575removed-- ==>
576removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
577removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
578removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
579removed-- ==>...`
580removed--
581removed-- So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too board, causing
582removed-- this lemma repeating itself. First we have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is
583removed-- defeq to (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m to be a
584removed-- TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this lemma applies again --
585removed-- `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]` which is
586removed-- `(MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]` and keep going.
587removed
588removed-- #### Updating
589removed
590removed-- More interesting is the map-updating function, which (as always) takes a
591removed-- map `m`, a key `a`, and a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to
592removed-- `b` and takes every other key to whatever `m` does. The novelty here is
593removed-- that we achieve this effect by wrapping a new function around the old one.
594removed
595removeddef update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β :=
596removed fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
597removed
598removed-- This definition is a nice example of higher-order programming: `update`
599removed-- takes a function `m` and yields a new function `fun x' ↦ ...` that behaves
600removed-- like the desired map.
601removed
602removed-- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where `"foo"`
603removed-- and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped to `false`,
604removed-- like this:
605removed
606removeddef exampleMap :=
607removed (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
608removed |>.update "foo" true
609removed |>.update "bar" true
610removed
611removed-- We'll also introduce a notation for updating maps
612removed
613removednotation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
614removed
615removedtheorem update_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
616removed a →ₜ b ; m = fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := rfl
617removed
618removed-- We can also hide the last case when it is empty:
619removed
620removednotation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
621removed
622removed-- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
623removed
624removeddef exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
625removeddef exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
626removed
627removed-- This completes the definition of total maps.
628removed
629removedexample : exampleMap = exampleMap' := rfl
630removedexample : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := rfl
631removed
632removedexample : exampleMap'["baz"] = false := rfl
633removedexample : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := rfl
634removedexample : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := rfl
635removedexample : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := rfl
636removed
637removed-- When we use maps in later chapters, we'll need several fundamental facts
638removed-- about how they behave.
639removed
640removed-- Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure you thoroughly
641removed-- understand the statements of the lemmas!
642removed
643removed-- (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality axiom, which was
644removed-- discussed in the Logic chapter.)
645removed
646removed-- First, the empty map returns its default element for all keys:
647removed
648removedtheorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := rfl
649removed
650removed-- Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new value `b` and then
651removed-- look up `a` in the map resulting from the `update`, we get back `b`:
652removed
653removedtheorem update_eq (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
654removed rw [update_def, getElem_def, ReflBEq.rfl, cond_true]
655removed
656removed-- On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁` and then look up a
657removed-- *different* key `a₂` in the resulting map, we get the same result that `m`
658removed-- would have given:
659removed
660removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_neq ⭐⭐
661removed
662removedtheorem update_neq {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
663removed (a₁ →ₜ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
664removed sorry
665removed
666removed-- The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we first need to
667removed-- say when two maps are equal. Since a total map *is* a function, this is
668removed-- exactly the functional extensionality principle from the Logic chapter: two
669removed-- maps are equal when they agree at every key. Recording it once, for maps,
670removed-- and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the `ext` tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to
671removed-- the pointwise one in the proofs below.
672removed
673removed@[ext]
674removedtheorem ext {m₁ m₂ : TotalMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := funext h
675removed
676removed-- If we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a value `b₁` and then update again
677removed-- with the same key `a` and another value `b₂`, the resulting map behaves the
678removed-- same (gives the same result when applied to any key) as the simpler map
679removed-- obtained by performing just the second `update` on `m`:
680removed
681removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_shadow ⭐⭐
682removed
683removedtheorem update_shadow (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
684removed (a →ₜ b₂ ; a →ₜ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₜ b₂ ; m) := by
685removed sorry
686removed
687removed-- Given keys `a₁` and `a₂`, the tactic `by_cases` `h : a₁ = a₂` splits the
688removed-- proof into the case where they are equal — where `subst h` then replaces
689removed-- one by the other — and the case where they are not, which is what
690removed-- `update_neq` wants. Use it to prove the following theorem, which states
691removed-- that if we update a map to assign key `a` the same value as it already has
692removed-- in `m`, then the result is equal to `m`:
693removed
694removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1, NOW):
695removed-- Two things the Rocq source says here have been dropped.
696removed--
697removed-- Rocq frames this case analysis around `destruct (eqb_spec x1 x2)`,
698removed-- which "simultaneously performs case analysis on the result of
699removed-- `String.eqb x1 x2` and generates hypotheses about the equality (in the
700removed-- sense of `=`) of `x1` and `x2`" — the boolean/propositional reflection
701removed-- idiom. The paragraph above replaces that with `by_cases`/`subst`, which
702removed-- is what the Lean proof uses. But reflection is what the `Reflection`
703removed-- section **below** is about, so the two may want to be connected rather
704removed-- than have one silently displace the other.
705removed--
706removed-- Rocq then says "With the example in chapter **IndProp** as a template,
707removed-- use `String.eqb_spec` to prove ...". That cross-reference is dropped,
708removed-- since it is unclear what the Lean `IndProp` chapter will end up
709removed-- containing. Revisit later.
710removed
711removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_same ⭐⭐
712removed
713removedtheorem update_same (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : (a →ₜ m[a] ; m) = m := by
714removed sorry
715removed
716removed-- Similarly, prove one final property of the `update` function: if we update
717removed-- a map `m` at two distinct keys, it doesn't matter in which order we do the
718removed-- updates.
719removed
720removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1, NOW):
721removed-- Rocq says "Similarly, use `String.eqb_spec` to prove ..."; the
722removed-- instruction to use a specific lemma is dropped here for the same reason
723removed-- as in the note above.
724removed
725removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): update_permute ⭐⭐⭐
726removed
727removedtheorem update_permute {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
728removed (a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; m) := by
729removed sorry
730removed
731removed-- Note to developers:
732removed-- The Rocq source also has `getElem_empty` (originally `apply_empty`) and
733removed-- `update_eq` as (optional) exercises; here they are worked examples,
734removed-- since `update_eq` was already presented that way. Reconsider if this
735removed-- section is rebalanced.
736removed
737removedend TotalMap
738removed
739removed-- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
740removed
741removed-- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation for concrete
742removed-- maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To accomplish this we define a
743removed-- simple structure that consists of a key and a value along with `↦` notation
744removed-- for it.
745removed
746removed/--
747removedA key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
748removed-/
749removed@[ext]
750removedstructure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
751removed key : K
752removed value : V
753removed
754removednamespace KVPair
755removedscoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
756removedend KVPair
757removed
758removedopen scoped KVPair
759removed
760removed-- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances which control the `{}`
761removed-- notation in lean.
762removed
763removednamespace TotalMap
764removed
765removedvariable [Inhabited β]
766removed
767removedinstance : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
768removed insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
769removed
770removedinstance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
771removed singleton kv := insert kv ∅
772removed
773removedinstance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
774removed insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
775removed
776removedend TotalMap
777removed
778removed-- Here are a couple of examples using the new notation:
779removed
780removedexample : ({ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }) = "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅ := rfl
781removed
782removedexample : ({ "foo" ↦ true } : TotalMap String Bool)["foo"] = true := rfl
783removed
784removedexample : ({ 1 ↦ 2, 1 ↦ 3 } : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = 2 := rfl
785removed
786removed-- The reason we need to explicitly specify the type of the map is that Lean
787removed-- doesn't know what type of collection `{ "foo" ↦ true }` is without type
788removed-- hints, as we can see with `#check`:
789removed
790removed#check { "foo" ↦ true }
791removed
792removed-- {"foo" ↦ true} : ?m.4
793removed
794removed-- The type shows a `?m.4`, which indicates that Lean can't infer the type. A
795removed-- type which can't be inferred doesn't have any type classes like
796removed-- `MyGetElem`, so typeclass resolution gets stuck in the following example:
797removed
798removedsf_expect_failure
799removed example : ({ "foo" ↦ true })["foo"] = true := rfl
800removed
801removed-- ### Partial Maps
802removed
803removed-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
804removed-- We should spend some time discussing differences between the inductive
805removed-- approach in Lists.lean and the approach here. The inductive approach
806removed-- could be made polymorphic and proven to be equivalent with partial maps
807removed-- (I believe), so the point is not that the maps are extensionally
808removed-- different. A question (that I don't have an answer to) is then: what
809removed-- makes the new partial map better?
810removed
811removed-- Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A partial map with
812removed-- elements of type `β` is simply a total map with elements of type
813removed-- `Option β`, whose default element is `none`.
814removed
815removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
816removed-- I don't understand the comment on the `inner` field...
817removed--
818removed-- Niklas Halonen (xhalo32): This is just a technical note that
819removed-- discourages using `PartialMap.inner` over `PartialMap.toTotal`. We
820removed-- don't want both to appear in the public API. Compare with
821removed-- `MeasurableSet'` in
822removed-- https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/1f8806b67d6f09e6d2552c031e6d3a3171016116/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/MeasurableSpace/Defs.lean#L52
823removed-- which doesn't appear in the public API (it uses `MeasurableSet`
824removed-- instead).
825removed
826removedstructure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
827removed /-- The inner total map. Should not appear in the public API, use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead. -/
828removed inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
829removed
830removedinstance : EmptyCollection (PartialMap α β) where
831removed emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }
832removed
833removeddef PartialMap.toTotal (m : PartialMap α β) : TotalMap α (Option β) := m.inner
834removed
835removedinstance : MyGetElem (PartialMap α β) α (Option β) where
836removed getElem m a := m.toTotal[a]
837removed
838removedtheorem getElem_def (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.toTotal[a] := rfl
839removed
840removed-- Remember that we discussed earlier with total maps that using function
841removed-- application exposes the implementation, and that's why we introduced a new
842removed-- notation `MyGetElem`? Here we take that concept to a new level, and instead
843removed-- of using a `def` for partial maps, like this...
844removed
845removed-- def PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := TotalMap α (Option β)`
846removed
847removed-- ...we define partial maps as a structure containing just a total map. This
848removed-- more strongly hides the fact that it's a total map.
849removed
850removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
851removed-- If this way is better, then why didn't we do it for total maps too?
852removed-- Just for the sake of explaining two different mechanisms? We should
853removed-- explain our reasoning.
854removed
855removed-- Now, the type system doesn't consider `PartialMap α β` to be definitionally
856removed-- equal to `TotalMap α (Option β)`, so the following equality doesn't type
857removed-- check:
858removed
859removedsf_expect_failure
860removed example : (∅ : PartialMap α β) = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := by rfl
861removed
862removed-- Type mismatch
863removed-- ∅
864removed-- has type
865removed-- TotalMap α (Option β)
866removed-- but is expected to have type
867removed-- PartialMap α β
868removed
869removed-- Note to developers (Claude, NOW):
870removed-- The Maps chapter removed the `optionCoe` instance for the duration of
871removed-- its partial-map development (`attribute [-instance] optionCoe`,
872removed-- restored at `end PartialMap`), on the grounds that a coercion from `β`
873removed-- to `Option β` might be confusing at this point. It also recorded two
874removed-- things about doing so: the removal must not leak to end-of-file, or
875removed-- Verso's `tag`/`file` metadata coercion (`Tag → Option Tag`) fails at
876removed-- end-of-document; and `[-instance]` cannot be scoped `local`, hence the
877removed-- manual add/restore pair.
878removed--
879removed-- We have not carried that over — nothing here needs it and it is not
880removed-- clear it is wanted. Decide whether to reinstate it.
881removed
882removed-- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value there. To
883removed-- update, we create a new partial map from `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by
884removed-- wrapping it in angle brackets, i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax.
885removed-- This is equivalent to writing `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We
886removed-- also introduce a similar notation for it as for total maps.
887removed
888removednamespace PartialMap
889removed
890removeddef update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : PartialMap α β :=
891removed ⟨a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal⟩
892removed
893removednotation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => PartialMap.update m a b
894removed
895removednotation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 => PartialMap.update ∅ a b
896removed
897removeddef examplePmap : PartialMap String Bool := "Church" →ₚ true ; "Turing" →ₚ false
898removed
899removed-- Next, we provide some fundamental properties about `toTotal`:
900removed
901removedtheorem toTotal_empty : (∅ : PartialMap α β).toTotal = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := rfl
902removed
903removedtheorem toTotal_update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
904removed (a →ₚ b ; m).toTotal = a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal := rfl
905removed
906removed-- As an example, here's how we can use these on some concrete maps:
907removed
908removedexample : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by
909removed rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_def]
910removed rfl
911removed
912removed-- This also holds by definition (`rfl`), since all the rewrites in the above
913removed-- proof do the computation step-by-step.
914removed
915removedexample : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by rfl
916removed
917removed-- Next, we lift all of the basic lemmas about total maps to partial maps. To
918removed-- do this we should first prove an extensionality lemma about partial maps.
919removed-- To prove extensionality, we employ injectivity of `PartialMap`'s
920removed-- constructor `mk` using `mk.injEq`.
921removed
922removedtheorem toTotal_eq_iff (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : m₁.toTotal = m₂.toTotal ↔ m₁ = m₂ := by
923removed rw [mk.injEq]
924removed rfl
925removed
926removed@[ext]
927removedtheorem ext {m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := by
928removed rw [← toTotal_eq_iff]
929removed exact TotalMap.ext h
930removed
931removed-- Now, let's lift the `TotalMap` lemmas:
932removed
933removedtheorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : PartialMap α β)[a] = none := by
934removed rw [getElem_def, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_empty, Option.default_eq_none]
935removed
936removedtheorem update_eq (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₚ b ; m)[a] = some b := by
937removed rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, TotalMap.update_eq]
938removed
939removedtheorem update_neq {m : PartialMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
940removed (a₁ →ₚ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
941removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
942removed rw [TotalMap.update_neq h]
943removed
944removedtheorem update_shadow (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
945removed (a →ₚ b₂ ; a →ₚ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₚ b₂ ; m) := by
946removed apply ext
947removed intro x
948removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
949removed rw [TotalMap.update_shadow]
950removed
951removedtheorem update_same {m : PartialMap α β} {a : α} {b : β} (h : m[a] = some b) :
952removed (a →ₚ b ; m) = m := by
953removed apply ext
954removed intro x
955removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
956removed rw [← h, getElem_def, TotalMap.update_same]
957removed
958removedtheorem update_permute {m : PartialMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
959removed (a₁ →ₚ b₁ ; a₂ →ₚ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₚ b₂ ; a₁ →ₚ b₁ ; m) := by
960removed apply ext
961removed intro x
962removed dsimp [getElem_def, toTotal_update]
963removed rw [TotalMap.update_permute h]
964removed
965removed-- And let's add `{}`-notation for partial maps as well.
966removed
967removedinstance : Insert (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
968removed insert kv m := kv.key →ₚ kv.value ; m
969removed
970removedinstance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
971removed singleton kv := insert kv ∅
972removed
973removedinstance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (PartialMap α β) where
974removed insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
975removed
976removedexample : { 1 ↦ 2, 2 ↦ 3 } = 1 →ₚ 2 ; 2 →ₚ 3 := rfl
977removed
978removed-- One last thing: for partial maps, it's convenient to introduce a notion of
979removed-- map inclusion, stating that all the entries in one map are also present in
980removed-- another. Lean already has notation for this — `m₁ ⊆ m₂` — which we get by
981removed-- supplying a `HasSubset` instance.
982removed
983removed-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
984removed-- I think it would be more idiomatic to define `Subset` as
985removed-- `∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b`.
986removed
987removeddef Subset (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : Prop :=
988removed ∀ (a : α) (b : β), m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b
989removed
990removedinstance : HasSubset (PartialMap α β) where
991removed Subset := PartialMap.Subset
992removed
993removedtheorem subset_def (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) :
994removed m₁ ⊆ m₂ ↔ (∀ (a : α) (b : β), m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b) := .rfl
995removed
996removed-- We can then show that map update preserves map inclusion, that is:
997removed
998removedtheorem update_subset (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) (h : m₁ ⊆ m₂) :
999removed (a →ₚ b ; m₁) ⊆ (a →ₚ b ; m₂) := by
1000removed rw [subset_def] at h ⊢
1001removed intro a' b' hb
1002removed by_cases ha : a = a'
1003removed · subst ha
1004removed rw [update_eq] at hb ⊢
1005removed exact hb
1006removed · rw [update_neq ha] at hb ⊢
1007removed exact h a' b' hb
1008removed
1009removedend PartialMap

1025removed-- ## Reflection
1026removed
1027removed-- Note to developers:
1028removed-- I think this will still exist in previous chapters, just not have the
1029removed-- reflection explanations until here? Since I can't import these yet,
1030removed-- just placing here at the top of this section — CGH Burtonpatel: These
1031removed-- definitions of even as boolean computation and Prop should go below,
1032removed-- after the table where we explain the difference.
1033removed
1034removednamespace Nat
1035removed
1036removed@[irreducible]
1037removeddef isEven : Nat → Bool
1038removed| 0 => true
1039removed| 1 => false
1040removed| n + 2 => isEven n
1041removed
1042removed@[irreducible]
1043removeddef double : Nat → Nat
1044removed| 0 => 0
1045removed| n + 1 => double n + 2
1046removed
1047removedsection
1048removed
1049removedunseal isEven
1050removedunseal double
1051removed
1052removedtheorem isEven_zero : isEven 0 = true := rfl
1053removedtheorem isEven_one : isEven 1 = false := rfl
1054removedtheorem isEven_succ_succ (n : Nat) : isEven (n + 2) = isEven n := rfl
1055removed
1056removedtheorem double_zero : double 0 = 0 := by rfl
1057removedtheorem double_succ (n : Nat) : double (n + 1) = double n + 2 := rfl
1058removed
1059removedend
1060removed
1061removeddef Even (n : Nat) := ∃ m, n = double m
1062removed
1063removedtheorem isEven_succ (n : Nat) : isEven (n + 1) = ! isEven n := by
1064removed induction n with
1065removed | zero =>
1066removed rewrite [Nat.zero_add, isEven_zero, isEven_one]
1067removed rfl
1068removed | succ n ih =>
1069removed rewrite [isEven_succ_succ, ih, Bool.not_not]
1070removed rfl
1071removed
1072removed-- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
1073removed-- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1074removed
1075removed-- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1076removed
1077removed-- - ⠀
1078removed-- - `Bool`
1079removed-- - `Prop`
1080removed-- - decidable?
1081removed-- - yes
1082removed-- - no
1083removed-- - useable with `match`?
1084removed-- - yes
1085removed-- - no
1086removed-- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1087removed-- - no
1088removed-- - yes
1089removed
1090removed-- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1091removed-- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1092removed-- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1093removed-- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1094removed
1095removed-- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1096removed-- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1097removed-- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1098removed-- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1099removed-- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1100removed
1101removed-- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1102removed-- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1103removed-- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1104removed-- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
1105removed-- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
1106removed-- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
1107removed-- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1108removed
1109removed-- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1110removed-- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
1111removed-- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1112removed-- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1113removed-- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
1114removed-- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
1115removed-- or as a function into Prop.
1116removed
1117removed-- As an example, we can write
1118removed
1119removedunseal isEven in
1120removedexample : isEven 42 := rfl
1121removed
1122removed-- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1123removed
1124removedunseal double in
1125removedexample : Even 42 := by exists 21
1126removed
1127removed-- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1128removed-- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1129removed
1130removed-- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
1131removed
1132removedtheorem even_double (k : Nat) : isEven (double k) = true := by
1133removed induction k with
1134removed | zero =>
1135removed rewrite [double_zero, isEven_zero]
1136removed rfl
1137removed | succ n ih =>
1138removed rewrite [double_succ, isEven_succ_succ]
1139removed exact ih
1140removed
1141removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): isEven_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1142removed
1143removedtheorem isEven_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1144removed ∃ k, n = bif isEven n then double k else double k + 1 := by sorry
1145removed
1146removed-- Now the main theorem:
1147removed
1148removedtheorem isEven_iff_Even {n : Nat} : isEven n = true ↔ Even n where
1149removed mp h := by
1150removed have ⟨k, hk⟩ := isEven_double_exists n
1151removed rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1152removed subst hk
1153removed exists k
1154removed mpr h := by
1155removed obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1156removed subst hk
1157removed exact even_double k
1158removed
1159removed-- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean computation `isEven n`
1160removed-- is reflected in the truth of the proposition `∃ k, n = double k`.
1161removed
1162removed-- Similarly, to state that two numbers n and m are equal, we can say either
1163removed
1164removed-- - that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1165removed-- - that `n = m`
1166removed
1167removed-- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1168removed
1169removed-- Note to developers:
1170removed-- This proof is from the typeclass version, which makes more sense if
1171removed-- maps are included — CGH
1172removed
1173removedexample (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : n₁ == n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂ := beq_iff_eq
1174removed
1175removed-- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized as
1176removed-- either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we choose?
1177removed
1178removed-- In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to do with the
1179removed-- *computational* nature of Lean's core language, which is designed so that
1180removed-- every function it expresses is total, and by default computable unless we
1181removed-- explicit indicate otherwise. As an example, consider trying to write a
1182removed-- function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an arbitrary type:
1183removed
1184removed-- Note to developers:
1185removed-- dsainati12 days ago We use regular if for the first time here. It is
1186removed-- probably necessary to explain at this point what if is and how it
1187removed-- differs from bif.
1188removed--
1189removed-- 👍 1 berberman1 day ago Should we clarify the difference between = and
1190removed-- ==? Observably if and bif can possibly accept both as the condition
1191removed-- because of Coe or DecidableEq instances, which IMO could be confusing.
1192removed--
1193removed-- Probably we can talk a bit about the coercion system in this file as
1194removed-- well, since Coe could be an example of typeclasses, so long as if we
1195removed-- ignore the outParam thing...
1196removed--
1197removed-- chenson20181 day ago I definitely intended for this to cover = versus
1198removed-- ==. Maps uses LawfulBEq (which says = and == coincide). If that will
1199removed-- now appear here it's a good place to give some more detail?
1200removed--
1201removed-- rogerburtonpatel1 day ago I think right after this part on decidability
1202removed-- is good. It's a hefty chunk of information already, so keeping distinct
1203removed-- ideas distinct is more likely than not a good call.
1204removed
1205removed-- Note to developers:
1206removed-- @dsainati - commenting this out for the same reason as above
1207removed--
1208removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1209removed--
1210removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1211removed--
1212removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1213removed
1214removed-- Lean will complain here that it cannot find an instance of `Decidable`.
1215removed-- This typeclass
1216removed
1217removed-- Note to developers:
1218removed-- @dsainati - commenting this out because the -keep doesn't work during
1219removed-- extraction; this causes Lean to get the two instances (the real one and
1220removed-- this one) confused
1221removed--
1222removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1223removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1224removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1225removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1226removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1227removed--
1228removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1229removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1230removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1231removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1232removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1233removed--
1234removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1235removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1236removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1237removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1238removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1239removed
1240removed-- is the way that we express in Lean that a given proposition is decidable.
1241removed-- This is the generalization of our observation that `isEven_iff_Even` was
1242removed-- reflecting a proof between boolean and propositional equality. In fact, we
1243removed-- can use this theorem to directly construct a `Decidable` instance
1244removed
1245removedinstance (n : Nat) : Decidable (Even n) := decidable_of_decidable_of_iff isEven_iff_Even
1246removed
1247removed-- Now we are able to complete such proofs by computation using the `decide`
1248removed-- tactic:
1249removed
1250removedsection
1251removedunseal isEven
1252removed
1253removedexample : Even 2 := by decide
1254removedexample : Even 4 := by decide
1255removedexample : Even 6 := by decide
1256removedexample : Even 100 := by decide
1257removedexample : ¬ Even 101 := by decide
1258removedexample : ∀ n < 10, Even (2 * n) := by decide
1259removedexample : ∀ n < 10, Even (2 * n) ∧ ¬ Even (2 * n + 1) := by decide
1260removedend
1261removed
1262removed-- In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis with `Decidable` in
1263removed-- order to determine when it is appropriate to use `Prop` and `Bool`
1264removed-- interchangeably. For instance, while our example `eq` failed above while
1265removed-- trying to use propositional equality `=` in the condition of an `if`
1266removed-- statement, we are allowed to write
1267removed
1268removeddef nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1269removed
1270removed-- Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of natural numbers is
1271removed-- decidable, and Lean makes use of this fact. If we print this definition
1272removed-- with notation unset, we would find that it is using `instDecidableEqNat`
1273removed
1274removedset_option pp.all true in
1275removed#print nat_eq
1276removed
1277removed-- which proves that this equality is decidable.
1278removed
1279removed-- This is only half the story however: while Lean's core theory enables this
1280removed-- computation, Lean is also often used in applications where we don't care
1281removed-- about computability, such as pure mathematics. In particular, it is
1282removed-- possible to write a function for arbitrary equality:
1283removed
1284removedsf_experiment
1285removed open scoped Classical in
1286removed noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1287removed
1288removed set_option pp.all true in
1289removed #print eq
1290removed
1291removed-- But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable` keyword and
1292removed-- `Classical` namespace that we are *not* interested in computation. What is
1293removed-- happening in the background is that this allows typeclass synthesis to find
1294removed-- the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which makes use of the axiom
1295removed-- of choice to provide a proof that all propositions are *classically*
1296removed-- decidable. This sort of definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is
1297removed-- not allowed to be used in conjunction with computational features of Lean
1298removed-- such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval` command.
1299removed

11removed-- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12removed-- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13removed-- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14removed-- through spanshot tasks.
15removedprivate def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16removed match (← get).scopes with
17removed | [] => act
18removed | h :: t =>
19removed let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20removed try
21removed orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22removed modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23removed act
24removed finally
25removed if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26removed let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27removed modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28removed
29removedprivate def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30removed let savedState ← get
31removed try
32removed m
33removed finally
34removed let state ← get
35removed set { savedState with
36removed -- Preserve the info tree
37removed infoState := state.infoState
38removed messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39removed
40removednamespace IndentedCommands
41removed
42removed/-! # Block Commands Parser
43removed Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44removed Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45removed we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46removed because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47removed One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48removed and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49removed-/
50removed
51removedopen Parser
52removed
53removedprivate def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54removed eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55removed
56removed/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57removedprivate def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58removed takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59removed
60removed/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61removed If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62removed requiring the indentation.
63removed-/
64removedprivate def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65removed takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66removed (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67removed (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68removed
69removedprivate def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70removed rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71removed
72removedprivate def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73removed
74removed@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75removedprivate def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76removed
77removed@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78removedprivate def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79removed
80removedprivate partial def runRawCmdsAux
81removed (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82removed let state ← get
83removed let scope := state.scopes.head!
84removed let pctx := {
85removed env := state.env
86removed options := scope.opts
87removed currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88removed openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89removed }
90removed let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91removed modify fun state => { state with messages }
92removed unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93removed elabCommand cmd
94removed runLinters cmd
95removed unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96removed runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97removed
98removed/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99removedprivate def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100removed let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101removed | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102removed let fileName ← getFileName
103removed let fileMap ← getFileMap
104removed -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105removed -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106removed -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107removed let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108removed if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109removed let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110removed (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111removed runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112removed else
113removed throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114removed
115removedend IndentedCommands
116removed
117removedend

176removeddef elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177removed let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178removed unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179removed throwUnsupportedSyntax
180removed let tk := stx[0]
181removed let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182removed commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183removed withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body

185removedend
