1removedimport TS.SFLCompat
2removed
3removed-- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4removed
5removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6removed-- We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7removed-- proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8removed-- width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9removed
10removed-- We begin by looking at a language we call **Slang** (for *simple
11removed-- language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets us introduce key concepts
12removed-- for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics* of programming languages and
13removed-- show how those concepts are realized in Lean.
14removed
15removed-- (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
16removed-- Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked through
17removed-- it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next chapter of
18removed-- this one.)
19removed
20removed-- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
21removed
22removed-- Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
23removed-- sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
24removed
25removed-- ### Syntax
26removed
27removednamespace Slang
28removed
29removed-- These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
30removed-- boolean expressions.
31removed
32removedinductive Aexp where
33removed | num (n : Nat)
34removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
35removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
36removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
37removed
38removedinductive Bexp where
39removed | bool (b : Bool)
40removed | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
41removed | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
42removed | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
43removed | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
44removed | not (b : Bexp)
45removed | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
46removed
47removed-- In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete syntax*
48removed-- that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax trees --
49removed-- the process that, for example, would translate the string `"1 + 2 * 3"` to
50removed-- the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
51removed
52removed-- For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
53removed-- defining the same abstract syntax:
54removed
55removed-- a ::= nat
56removed-- | a + a
57removed-- | a − a
58removed-- | a * a
59removed-- b ::= bool
60removed-- | a = a
61removed-- | a ≠ a
62removed-- | a ≤ a
63removed-- | a > a
64removed-- | ¬ b
65removed-- | b ∧ b
66removed
67removed-- Compared to the Lean version above...
68removed
69removed-- - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions about
70removed-- the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the addition
71removed-- operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other aspects of
72removed-- lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence of `+`, `-`, and
73removed-- `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions, etc.) unspecified. Some
74removed-- additional information -- and human intelligence -- would be required to
75removed-- turn this description into a formal definition, e.g., for implementing a
76removed-- compiler. The Lean version consistently omits all this information and
77removed-- concentrates on the abstract syntax only.
78removed
79removed-- - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its informality
80removed-- makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like discussions at the
81removed-- blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more important than nailing
82removed-- down every detail precisely.
83removed
84removed-- Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch freely
85removed-- among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of BNF they're
86removed-- using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready informal
87removed-- understanding is all that's important.
88removed
89removed-- It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones for
90removed-- communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
91removed-- implementations and proofs.
92removed
93removed-- ### Evaluation
94removed
95removed-- *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
96removed
97removeddef Aexp.eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
98removed match a with
99removed | num n => n
100removed | plus a1 a2 => a1.eval + a2.eval
101removed | minus a1 a2 => a1.eval - a2.eval
102removed | mult a1 a2 => a1.eval * a2.eval
103removed
104removed-- By convention, we pair the definition with one *simplification lemma* per
105removed-- constructor, specifying how `eval` behaves on that constructor. Proofs then
106removed-- rewrite by these lemmas rather than peeking through the definition of
107removed-- `eval`. We tag each lemma `@[simp]`, so `simp` applies them automatically.
108removed
109removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
110removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (plus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval + a2.eval := rfl
111removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (minus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval - a2.eval := rfl
112removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (mult a1 a2).eval = a1.eval * a2.eval := rfl
113removed
114removedexample : Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
115removed
116removed-- Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean, and we give it
117removed-- the same treatment.
118removed
119removeddef Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
120removed match b with
121removed | bool b => b
122removed | eq a1 a2 => a1.eval == a2.eval
123removed | neq a1 a2 => a1.eval != a2.eval
124removed | le a1 a2 => a1.eval ≤ a2.eval
125removed | gt a1 a2 => a1.eval > a2.eval
126removed | not b1 => !eval b1
127removed | and b1 b2 => eval b1 && eval b2
128removed
129removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
130removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (eq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval == a2.eval) := rfl
131removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (neq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval != a2.eval) := rfl
132removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (le a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval ≤ a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
133removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (gt a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval > a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
134removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
135removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (b1 b2 : Bexp) : (and b1 b2).eval = (b1.eval && b2.eval) := rfl
136removed
137removed-- It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
138removed-- `a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval` returns a
139removed-- `Bool` so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide` coercion. You can observe the
140removed-- call to `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and `Bexp.eval_gt`.
141removed
142removed-- _Quiz:_
143removed
144removed-- What does the following expression evaluate to?
145removed
146removed-- Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
147removed
148removed-- (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
149removed
150removed-- ### Optimization
151removed
152removed-- We can now start to get some mileage out of these definitions. Suppose we
153removed-- define a function that takes an arithmetic expression and slightly
154removed-- simplifies it, changing every occurrence of `0 + e` (i.e.,
155removed-- `.plus (.num 0) e`) into just `e`.
156removed
157removeddef Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
158removed match a with
159removed | num n => num n
160removed | plus (num 0) e2 => optimize0plus e2
161removed | plus e1 e2 => plus (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
162removed | minus e1 e2 => minus (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
163removed | mult e1 e2 => mult (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
164removed
165removed-- To gain confidence that our optimization is doing the right thing we can
166removed-- test it on some examples and see if the output looks OK.
167removed
168removedexample :
169removed Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
170removed (.plus (.num 0)
171removed (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
172removed = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
173removed
174removed-- But if we want to be certain the optimization is correct -- that evaluating
175removed-- an optimized expression *always* gives the same result as the original --
176removed-- we should prove it!
177removed
178removed-- Here is a first, deliberately explicit, proof, by induction on `a`. The
179removed-- interesting case is `plus`: because `optimize0plus` treats `plus (num 0) e`
180removed-- specially, we case-split on the left operand `a1` -- and, when it is a
181removed-- numeral, on whether that numeral is `0` -- to line the proof up with the
182removed-- function's own branches. Once the constructors are exposed, each case is
183removed-- discharged by essentially the same incantation: unfold `optimize0plus`,
184removed-- rewrite `eval` by its characterizing lemmas, then finish with the induction
185removed-- hypotheses. Notice how repetitive that makes the proof.
186removed
187removedtheorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
188removed a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
189removed induction a with
190removed | num n => rfl
191removed | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
192removed cases a1 with
193removed | num n =>
194removed cases n with
195removed | zero =>
196removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
197removed exact ih2
198removed | succ n =>
199removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
200removed rw [ih2]
201removed | plus b1 b2 =>
202removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
203removed rw [ih1, ih2]
204removed | minus b1 b2 =>
205removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
206removed rw [ih1, ih2]
207removed | mult b1 b2 =>
208removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
209removed rw [ih1, ih2]
210removed | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
211removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
212removed rw [ih1, ih2]
213removed | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
214removed simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
215removed rw [ih1, ih2]
216removed
217removed-- We can do much better. The case analysis we performed by hand -- peeling
218removed-- `plus` apart to reach the `plus (num 0) e` branch -- is exactly the case
219removed-- analysis that `optimize0plus` itself performs. The `fun_induction` tactic
220removed-- inducts along a function's **own** recursion structure:
221removed-- `fun_induction
222removed-- Aexp.optimize0plus a` hands us one goal per branch of
223removed-- `optimize0plus` -- the special `plus (num 0) e` branch included -- so the
224removed-- nested `cases` disappear.
225removed
226removed-- Every remaining goal now has the same shape, so we can attack them
227removed-- uniformly with the `<;>` combinator, which runs a single tactic on **all**
228removed-- the goals produced by the induction. That single tactic is `simp_all`: it
229removed-- rewrites `eval` by the `@[simp]` characterizing lemmas and uses the
230removed-- induction hypotheses -- which `simp_all` picks up from the local context
231removed-- automatically -- to close each goal. The whole proof collapses to two
232removed-- lines.
233removed
234removedtheorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
235removed a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
236removed fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
237removed
238removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
239removed
240removed-- Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change the value of
241removed-- an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all the `Aexp`s that appear in
242removed-- a `Bexp` without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a function that
243removed-- performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it sound. Use the
244removed-- combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short and elegant as
245removed-- possible.
246removed
247removeddef Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := sorry
248removed
249removedexample :
250removed Bexp.optimize0plusB
251removed (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
252removed = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := sorry
253removed
254removedexample :
255removed Bexp.optimize0plusB
256removed (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
257removed = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := sorry
258removed
259removedtheorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
260removed b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
261removed sorry
262removed
263removed-- ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize ⭐⭐⭐⭐
264removed
265removed-- The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is only one of
266removed-- many possible optimizations on arithmetic and boolean expressions. Write a
267removed-- more sophisticated optimizer and prove it correct. (You will probably find
268removed-- it easiest to start small -- add just a single, simple optimization and its
269removed-- correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to something more
270removed-- interesting.)
271removed
272removed-- ## Evaluation as a Relation
273removed
274removed-- We have presented `Aexp.eval` and `Bexp.eval` as functions defined by
275removed-- recursion. Another way to think about evaluation -- one that is often more
276removed-- flexible -- is as a *relation* between expressions and their values. This
277removed-- perspective leads to inductive definitions like the following.
278removed
279removedinductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
280removed | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
281removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
282removed EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
283removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
284removed EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
285removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
286removed EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
287removed
288removed-- One comment on the style of this definition. We could instead have
289removed-- presented this relation with **positional** hypotheses -- no names for the
290removed-- premises.
291removed
292removednamespace ArithUnnamed
293removed
294removedinductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
295removed | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
296removed | plus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.plus e1 e2) (n1 + n2)
297removed | minus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.minus e1 e2) (n1 - n2)
298removed | mult (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.mult e1 e2) (n1 * n2)
299removed
300removedend ArithUnnamed
301removed
302removed-- The version above makes the rules somewhat easier to read, but gives less
303removed-- control over naming the hypotheses during proofs involving the relation.
304removed-- For this reason we adopt the named style.
305removed
306removed-- It will be convenient to have an infix notation for `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll
307removed-- write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value
308removed-- `n`.
309removed
310removedscoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => Aexp.EvalR e n
311removed
312removed-- In Lean the `notation` is declared right after the inductive. The `scoped`
313removed-- keyword allows us to scope the notation to the present namespace so it
314removed-- doesn't collide with other evaluation relations later.
315removed
316removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
317removed-- The Rocq version here says "As we saw in our case study of regular
318removed-- expressions in chapter IndProp, Rocq provides a way to use this
319removed-- notation in the definition of aevalR itself." It then re-shows the
320removed-- definition with Downarrow. We need to resolve how we want to do this.
321removed
322removed-- ### Inference Rule Notation
323removed
324removed-- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
325removed-- `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form of
326removed-- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
327removed-- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like
328removed-- this as an inference rule:
329removed
330removed-- e1 ⇓ n1
331removed-- e2 ⇓ n2
332removed-- ------------------ (plus)
333removed-- plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
334removed
335removed-- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
336removed-- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
337removed
338removed-- | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) :
339removed-- EvalR a1 n1 →
340removed-- EvalR a2 n2 →
341removed-- EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
342removed
343removed-- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
344removed-- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
345removed-- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
346removed-- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
347removed-- variables mentioned in the rule (`e1`, `n1`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
348removed-- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
349removed-- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
350removed-- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
351removed-- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
352removed-- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
353removed-- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
354removed-- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
355removed
356removed-- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
357removed-- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
358removed-- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
359removed-- `e1` and `n1` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
360removed-- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:
361removed
362removed-- --------- (num)
363removed-- num n ⇓ n
364removed
365removed-- e1 ⇓ n1
366removed-- e2 ⇓ n2
367removed-- ------------------ (plus)
368removed-- plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
369removed
370removed-- e1 ⇓ n1
371removed-- e2 ⇓ n2
372removed-- ------------------- (minus)
373removed-- minus e1 e2 ⇓ n1-n2
374removed
375removed-- e1 ⇓ n1
376removed-- e2 ⇓ n2
377removed-- ------------------ (mult)
378removed-- mult e1 e2 ⇓ n1*n2
379removed
380removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
381removed-- The first two quizzes here seem kind of boring.
382removed
383removed-- _Quiz:_
384removed
385removed-- Which rules are needed to prove the following?
386removed
387removed-- .mult (.plus (.num 3) (.num 1)) (.num 0) ⇓ 0
388removed
389removed-- (A) `num` and `plus` (B) `num` only (C) `num` and `mult` (D) `mult` and
390removed-- `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`
391removed
392removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
393removed-- Not sure if we need ⇓b, or whether we can define ⇓ overloaded. Don't
394removed-- understand Lean notation yet!
395removed
396removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
397removed-- About `Bexp.eval` below: We should discuss a way to recall definitions
398removed-- without having to write them out manually like this. I think a simple
399removed-- `#print` may work as an alternative, assuming there are no namespace
400removed-- issues..
401removed
402removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): beval_rules ⭐
403removed
404removed-- Here, again, is the definition of the `Bexp.eval` function:
405removed
406removed-- def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
407removed-- match b with
408removed-- | bool b => b
409removed-- | eq a1 a2 => a1.eval == a2.eval
410removed-- | neq a1 a2 => a1.eval != a2.eval
411removed-- | le a1 a2 => a1.eval ≤ a2.eval
412removed-- | gt a1 a2 => a1.eval > a2.eval
413removed-- | not b1 => !eval b1
414removed-- | and b1 b2 => eval b1 && eval b2
415removed
416removed-- Write out a corresponding definition of boolean evaluation as a relation
417removed-- (in inference rule notation).
418removed
419removed-- ### Equivalence of the Definitions
420removed
421removed-- It is straightforward to prove that the relational and functional
422removed-- definitions of evaluation agree.
423removed
424removedtheorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
425removed a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
426removed constructor
427removed · intro h
428removed induction h with
429removed | num n => rfl
430removed | plus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
431removed | minus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
432removed | mult a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih1, ih2]
433removed · intro h
434removed subst h
435removed induction a with
436removed | num n => exact .num n
437removed | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .plus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
438removed | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .minus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
439removed | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .mult a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
440removed
441removed-- We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more automation like we did
442removed-- in the previous section.
443removed
444removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
445removed-- the `workinclass!` marker should signal this live in-class exercise.
446removed-- But it is not rendering properly on the HTML. In fact it replaces
447removed-- `workinclass!` with the `all_goals` tactic, which we don't need.
448removed
449removedtheorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
450removed a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
451removed all_goals
452removed constructor
453removed · intro h; induction h <;> simp_all
454removed · intro h; subst h; induction a <;> constructor <;> assumption
455removed
456removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): bevalR ⭐⭐⭐
457removed
458removed-- Write a relation `Bexp.EvalR` in the same style as `Aexp.EvalR`, and prove
459removed-- that it is equivalent to `Bexp.eval`.
460removed
461removedinductive Bexp.EvalR : Bexp → Bool → Prop where
462removed -- FILL IN HERE
463removed
464removedscoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓b " b:56 => Bexp.EvalR e b
465removed
466removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
467removed-- There is no keyboard shortcut for a subscript b, nor is there one for c
468removed-- (to use used with cevalR below). There are numbers, x, y, z, l, m, n,
469removed-- etc.
470removed
471removedtheorem Bexp.evalR_iff_eval (b : Bexp) (bv : Bool) :
472removed b ⇓b bv ↔ b.eval = bv := by
473removed sorry
474removed
475removedend Slang
476removed
477removed-- ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
478removed
479removed-- For the definitions of evaluation for arithmetic and boolean expressions,
480removed-- the choice of whether to use functional or relational definitions is mainly
481removed-- a matter of taste. However, there are situations where relational
482removed-- definitions work much better than functional ones.
483removed
484removednamespace Slang.AevalRDivision
485removed
486removed-- For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic operations
487removed-- with division:
488removed
489removedinductive Aexp where
490removed | num (n : Nat)
491removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
492removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
493removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
494removed | div (a1 a2 : Aexp) -- NEW
495removed
496removed-- Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new operation would
497removed-- not be straightforward due to division being a *partial* operation; i.e.,
498removed-- what should we return as the result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? By
499removed-- contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational version of the
500removed-- definition.
501removed
502removedinductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
503removed | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
504removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
505removed EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
506removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
507removed EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
508removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
509removed EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
510removed | div (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 n3 : Nat) -- NEW
511removed (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) (hpos : n2 > 0) (hdiv : n2 * n3 = n1) :
512removed EvalR (.div a1 a2) n3
513removed
514removed-- Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of 0) for which
515removed-- this relation does not specify an output.
516removed
517removedend Slang.AevalRDivision
518removed
519removednamespace Slang.AevalRExtended
520removed
521removed-- As another example, suppose that we want to extend the arithmetic
522removed-- operations by a nondeterministic number generator `any` that, when
523removed-- evaluated, may yield any number. (This is not the same as making a
524removed-- *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say which results are
525removed-- *possible*.)
526removed
527removedinductive Aexp where
528removed | any -- NEW
529removed | num (n : Nat)
530removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
531removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
532removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
533removed
534removed-- Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since evaluation is now *not*
535removed-- a deterministic function from expressions to numbers; but extending the
536removed-- relation is no problem.
537removed
538removedinductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
539removed | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n -- NEW
540removed | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
541removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
542removed EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
543removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
544removed EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
545removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
546removed EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
547removed
548removedend Slang.AevalRExtended
549removed
550removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
551removed-- The following text seems not quite right to me. First, you can use
552removed-- options for partial functions, and that's very natural to do in Lean as
553removed-- a monad. Second, and related, monadic functions need not even be
554removed-- terminating if the implement the `CCPO` typeclass and are labeled as a
555removed-- `partial_fixpoint`. Maybe we don't want to get into the second thing
556removed-- here, but failing to mention options (which I think were introduced in
557removed-- LF) seems a bit surprising.
558removed
559removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
560removed-- Agreed.
561removed
562removed-- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
563removed-- default?
564removed
565removed-- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function -- or is
566removed-- genuinely *not* a function -- there is no real choice. When both styles are
567removed-- workable, relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to
568removed-- understand, and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles
569removed-- from them. On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
570removed-- deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these
571removed-- if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify
572removed-- them during proofs.
573removed
574removed-- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
575removed-- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
576removed-- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above.
577removed
578removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
579removed-- Well, we didn't actually do a proof that switched between the points of
580removed-- view. Should we?
581removed
