51removed-- ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
52removed
53removed-- The evaluators we saw for Slang were formulated in a "big-step" style: they
54removed-- specify how a given expression can be evaluated to its final value "all in
55removed-- one big step":
56removed
57removed-- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
58removed
59removed-- This style is simple and natural for many purposes — indeed, Gilles Kahn,
60removed-- who popularized it, called it *natural semantics*. But there are some
61removed-- things it does not do well. In particular, it does not give us a convenient
62removed-- way of talking about *concurrent* programming languages, where the
63removed-- semantics of a program — the essence of how it behaves — includes not just
64removed-- which input states get mapped to which output states, but also the
65removed-- intermediate states that it passes through along the way; this is crucial,
66removed-- since these states can also be observed by concurrently executing code.
67removed
68removed-- Another shortcoming of the big-step style is more technical but equally
69removed-- critical in many situations. Suppose we want to define a variant of our
70removed-- expression language where a value could be *either* a number *or* a list of
71removed-- numbers. In the syntax of this extended language, it will be possible to
72removed-- write strange expressions like `2 + nil`, and our semantics for arithmetic
73removed-- expressions will then need to say something about how such expressions
74removed-- behave. One possibility is to maintain the convention that every arithmetic
75removed-- expression evaluates to some number by choosing some way of viewing a list
76removed-- as a number — e.g., by specifying that a list should be interpreted as `0`
77removed-- when it occurs in a context expecting a number. But this would be a bit of
78removed-- a hack.
79removed
80removed-- A much more natural approach is simply to say that the behavior of the
81removed-- expression `2 + nil` is *undefined* — i.e., it doesn't evaluate to any
82removed-- result at all. And we can easily do this: we just have to formulate `aeval`
83removed-- and `beval` as inductive propositions rather than functions, so that we can
84removed-- make them partial functions instead of total ones.
85removed
86removed-- Now, however, we encounter a subtlety that will become important once we
87removed-- move to a full programming language with looping. There, a program might
88removed-- fail to produce a result for *two quite different reasons*: either because
89removed-- the execution gets into an infinite loop or because, at some point, the
90removed-- program tries to do an operation that makes no sense, such as adding a
91removed-- number to a list, so that none of the evaluation rules can be applied.
92removed
93removed-- These two outcomes — nontermination vs. getting stuck in an erroneous
94removed-- configuration — should not be confused. In particular, we want to *allow*
95removed-- the first (because permitting the possibility of infinite loops is the
96removed-- price we pay for the convenience of programming with general looping
97removed-- constructs) but *prevent* the second (which is just wrong), for example by
98removed-- adding some form of *typechecking* to the language. Indeed, this will be a
99removed-- major topic of the next chapter, on *types*. As a first step, we need a way
100removed-- of presenting the semantics that allows us to distinguish nontermination
101removed-- from erroneous "stuck states."
102removed
103removed-- So, for lots of reasons, we'd like to have a finer-grained way of defining
104removed-- and reasoning about program behaviors. This is the topic of the present
105removed-- chapter. Our goal is to replace the "big-step" `Eval` relation with a
106removed-- "small-step" relation that specifies, for a given program, how its atomic
107removed-- steps of computation are performed. In the *small-step* style, we show how
108removed-- to "reduce" an expression to a simpler form by performing a single step of
109removed-- computation:
110removed
111removed-- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4
112removed-- ⟶ 2 + 2 + 12
113removed-- ⟶ 4 + 12
114removed-- ⟶ 16
115removed
116removed-- ## A Toy Language
117removed
118removed-- To save space, we start with an incredibly simple language of just
119removed-- constants and addition. (We use single-letter constructors `c` and `p` —
120removed-- for Constant and Plus — for brevity.) The same techniques scale up to
121removed-- richer languages.
122removed
123removedinductive Tm where
124removed | c (n : Nat) -- Constant
125removed | p (t1 t2 : Tm) -- Plus
126removed
127removed-- A standard big-step evaluator, as a function.
128removed
129removeddef evalF (t : Tm) : Nat :=
130removed match t with
131removed | .c n => n
132removed | .p t1 t2 => evalF t1 + evalF t2
133removed
134removed-- Here is the same evaluator, written in exactly the same style, but
135removed-- formulated as an inductively defined relation. We use the notation `t ⇓ n`
136removed-- for "`t` evaluates to `n`."
137removed
138removed-- The `notation` command below is how that is declared: it introduces `⇓` as
139removed-- infix syntax for the `Eval` relation defined with it, with a precedence
140removed-- saying how tightly it binds. This is the lightweight way to name a
141removed-- relation; later chapters, where a whole object language needs a grammar
142removed-- rather than a single operator, reach for `declare_syntax_cat` instead.
143removed
144removed-- ------- (const)
145removed-- c n ⇓ n
146removed
147removed-- t1 ⇓ n1
148removed-- t2 ⇓ n2
149removed-- ----------------- (plus)
150removed-- p t1 t2 ⇓ n1 + n2
151removed
152removedinductive Eval : Tm → Nat → Prop where
153removed | const (n : Nat) : Eval (.c n) n
154removed | plus (t1 t2 : Tm) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : Eval t1 n1) (h2 : Eval t2 n2) : Eval (.p t1 t2) (n1 + n2)
155removed
156removednotation:50 t " ⇓ " n => Eval t n
157removed
158removed-- Now, here is the corresponding *small-step* relation, written `t ⟶ t'`:
159removed
160removed-- ------------------------------- (plus)
161removed-- p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶ c (n1 + n2)
162removed
163removed-- t1 ⟶ t1'
164removed-- -------------------- (plusLeft)
165removed-- p t1 t2 ⟶ p t1' t2
166removed
167removed-- t2 ⟶ t2'
168removed-- ---------------------------- (plusRight)
169removed-- p (c n1) t2 ⟶ p (c n1) t2'
170removed
171removednamespace SimpleArith1
172removed
173removedinductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
174removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :
175removed Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
176removed | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm)
177removed (h : Step t1 t1') :
178removed Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
179removed | plusRight (n1 : Nat) (t2 t2' : Tm)
180removed (h : Step t2 t2') :
181removed Step (.p (.c n1) t2) (.p (.c n1) t2')
182removed
183removedscoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
184removed
185removed-- Things to notice:
186removed
187removed-- - We are defining a single reduction step, in which just one `p` node is
188removed-- replaced by its value.
189removed
190removed-- - Each step finds the *leftmost* `p` node that is ready to go (both of its
191removed-- operands are constants) and rewrites it in place. The first rule tells how
192removed-- to rewrite this `p` node itself; the other two rules tell how to find it.
193removed
194removed-- - A term that is just a constant cannot take a step.
195removed
196removed-- Let's pause and check a couple of examples of reasoning with the step
197removed-- relation.
198removed
199removed-- If `t1` steps to `t1'`, then `p t1 t2` steps to `p t1' t2`.
200removed
201removedexample :
202removed (.p
203removed (.p (.c 1) (.c 3))
204removed (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶
205removed (.p
206removed (.c 4)
207removed (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) := by
208removed apply Step.plusLeft; apply Step.plus
209removed
210removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): test_step_2 ⭐
211removed
212removed-- Right-hand sides step only once the left side is a value.
213removed
214removedexample :
215removed (.p
216removed (.c 0)
217removed (.p
218removed (.c 2)
219removed (.p
220removed (.c 1)
221removed (.c 3))))
222removed ⟶
223removed (.p
224removed (.c 0)
225removed (.p
226removed (.c 2)
227removed (.c 4))) := by
228removed sorry
229removed
230removed-- _Quiz:_
231removed
232removed-- To what does the following term step?
233removed
234removed-- .p
235removed-- (.p
236removed-- (.c 1)
237removed-- (.c 2))
238removed-- (.p
239removed-- (.c 1)
240removed-- (.c 2))
241removed
242removed-- (A) `.c 6` (B) `.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2))` (C)
243removed-- `.p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 3)` (D) `.p (.c 3) (.c 3)` (E) None of the above
244removed
245removed-- _Quiz:_
246removed
247removed-- What about this one?
248removed
249removed-- .c 1
250removed
251removed-- (A) `.c 1` (B) `.p (.c 0) (.c 1)` (C) None of the above
252removed
253removedend SimpleArith1
254removed
255removed-- ## Relations
256removed
257removed-- We will be working with several different single-step relations, so it is
258removed-- helpful to generalize a bit and state a few definitions and theorems about
259removed-- relations in general. (The optional chapter `Rel` in *Logical Foundations*
260removed-- develops some of these ideas in a bit more detail; reviewing that chapter
261removed-- may be useful if the treatment here feels too terse.)
262removed
263removed-- A *binary relation* on a type `X` is a family of propositions parameterized
264removed-- by two elements of `X` — i.e., a proposition about pairs of elements of
265removed-- `X`.
266removed
267removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
268removed-- Should we be getting this (and `Deterministic`, `Multi`, etc. if
269removed-- appropriate) from the Lean standard library? If not, should we match
270removed-- the concepts in CSLib, if they exists there?
271removed
272removeddef Relation (X : Type) := X → X → Prop
273removed
274removed-- Our main examples of such relations in this chapter will be the single-step
275removed-- reduction relation, `⟶`, and its multi-step variant, `⟶*`, defined below,
276removed-- but there are many other examples — e.g., the "equals," "less than," "less
277removed-- than or equal to," and "is the square of" relations on numbers, and the
278removed-- "prefix of" relation on lists and strings.
279removed
280removed-- One simple property a relation may have is being *deterministic*: like
281removed-- Slang's big-step evaluation, each element is related to at most one other.
282removed
283removed-- *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such that `t` steps to
284removed-- `t'`. We prove it by induction on the derivation of the first step.
285removed
286removed-- *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y1` and `y2`, then `y1`
287removed-- and `y2` are equal, by induction on a derivation of `x ⟶ y1`. There are
288removed-- several cases, depending on the last rule used in this derivation and the
289removed-- last rule in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y2`.
290removed
291removed-- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
292removed
293removed-- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight` follow
294removed-- by the induction hypothesis.
295removed
296removed-- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
297removed-- `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
298removed-- `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of
299removed-- `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
300removed
301removed-- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
302removed-- `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t1 t2` where
303removed-- `t1` has both the form `p t11 t12` and the form `c n`.
304removed
305removed-- Formally,
306removed
307removeddef Deterministic {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
308removed ∀ x y1 y2 : X, R x y1 → R x y2 → y1 = y2
309removed
310removednamespace SimpleArith2
311removed
312removedtheorem step_deterministic : Deterministic SimpleArith1.Step := by
313removed intro x y1 y2 h1
314removed induction h1 generalizing y2 with
315removed | plus n1 n2 =>
316removed intro h2
317removed cases h2 <;> first | rfl | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _›
318removed | plusLeft t1 t1' t2 hs ih =>
319removed intro h2
320removed cases h2 <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t1 _›]
321removed | plusRight n1 t2 t2' hs ih =>
322removed intro h2
323removed cases h2 <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t2 _›]
324removed
325removedend SimpleArith2
326removed
327removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
328removed-- In the Rocq there is the development of a special tactic to make this
329removed-- proof simpler. Do we want that here?
330removed
331removed-- ### Values
332removed
333removed-- Next, it will be useful to slightly reformulate the definition of
334removed-- single-step reduction by stating it in terms of "values."
335removed
336removed-- It can be useful to think of the `⟶` relation as defining an *abstract
337removed-- machine*:
338removed
339removed-- - At any moment, the *state* of the machine is a term.
340removed
341removed-- - A *step* of the machine is an atomic unit of computation — here, a single
342removed-- "add" operation.
343removed
344removed-- - The *halting states* of the machine are ones where there is no more
345removed-- computation to be done.
346removed
347removed-- We can then *execute* a term `t` as follows:
348removed
349removed-- - Take `t` as the starting state of the machine.
350removed
351removed-- - Repeatedly use the `⟶` relation to find a sequence of machine states,
352removed-- starting with `t`, where each state steps to the next.
353removed
354removed-- - When no more reduction is possible, "read out" the final state of the
355removed-- machine as the result of execution.
356removed
357removed-- Intuitively, it is clear that the final states of our machine are always
358removed-- terms of the form `c n` for some `n`. We call such terms *values*.
359removed
360removedinductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
361removed | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
362removed
363removed-- Having introduced the idea of values, we can use it in the definition of
364removed-- the `⟶` relation to write the `plusRight` rule in a slightly more elegant
365removed-- way.
366removed
367removed-- ------------------------------ (plus)
368removed-- p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶ c (n1 + n2)
369removed
370removed-- t1 ⟶ t1'
371removed-- ------------------- (plusLeft)
372removed-- p t1 t2 ⟶ p t1' t2
373removed
374removed-- IsValue v1
375removed-- t2 ⟶ t2'
376removed-- ------------------- (plusRight)
377removed-- p v1 t2 ⟶ p v1 t2'
378removed
379removed-- Again, the variable names in the informal presentation carry important
380removed-- information: by convention, `v1` ranges only over values, while `t1` and
381removed-- `t2` range over arbitrary terms.
382removed
383removed-- (Given this convention, the explicit `IsValue` hypothesis is arguably
384removed-- redundant, since the naming convention tells us where to add it when
385removed-- translating the informal rule to Lean. We'll keep it for now, to maintain a
386removed-- close correspondence between the informal and Lean versions of the rules,
387removed-- but later on we'll drop it in informal rules for brevity.)
388removed
389removed-- Here are the formal rules.
390removed
391removedinductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
392removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :
393removed Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
394removed | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm)
395removed (h : Step t1 t1') :
396removed Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
397removed | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm)
398removed (hv : IsValue v1)
399removed (h : Step t2 t2') :
400removed Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
401removed
402removednotation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
403removed
404removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): redo_determinism ⭐⭐⭐
405removed
406removed-- As a sanity check on this change, let's re-verify determinism. Here's an
407removed-- informal proof:
408removed
409removed-- *Proof sketch*: We must show that if `x` steps to both `y1` and `y2`, then
410removed-- `y1` and `y2` are equal. Consider the final rules used in the derivations
411removed-- of `x ⟶ y1` and `x ⟶ y2`.
412removed
413removed-- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
414removed
415removed-- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight` follow
416removed-- by the induction hypothesis.
417removed
418removed-- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
419removed-- `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
420removed-- `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of
421removed-- `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
422removed
423removed-- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
424removed-- `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t1 t2` where
425removed-- `t1` both has the form `p t11 t12` and is a value (hence has the form
426removed-- `c n`).
427removed
428removed-- Most of this proof is the same as the one above. But to get maximum benefit
429removed-- from the exercise you should try to write your formal version from scratch
430removed-- and just use the earlier one if you get stuck. The impossible cross-cases
431removed-- now also use the fact that a `IsValue` (a `c n`) cannot step.
432removed
433removedtheorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Step := by
434removed sorry
435removed
436removed-- ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
437removed
438removed-- The definition of single-step reduction for our toy language is fairly
439removed-- simple, but for a larger language it would be easy to forget one of the
440removed-- rules and accidentally create a situation where some term cannot take a
441removed-- step even though it has not been completely reduced to a value. The
442removed-- following theorem shows that we did not, in fact, make such a mistake here.
443removed
444removed-- *Theorem* (*Strong Progress*): If `t` is a term, then either `t` is a value
445removed-- or else there exists a term `t'` such that `t ⟶ t'`.
446removed
447removed-- *Proof*: By induction on `t`.
448removed
449removed-- - Suppose `t = c n`. Then `t` is a value.
450removed
451removed-- - Suppose `t = p t1 t2`, where (by the IH) `t1` either is a value or can step
452removed-- to some `t1'`, and where `t2` is either a value or can step to some `t2'`.
453removed-- We must show `p t1 t2` is either a value or steps to some `t'`.
454removed
455removed-- - If `t1` and `t2` are both values, then `t` can take a step, by `plus`.
456removed
457removed-- - If `t1` is a value and `t2` can take a step, then so can `t`, by
458removed-- `plusRight`.
459removed
460removed-- - If `t1` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `plusLeft`.
461removed
462removed-- Or, formally:
463removed
464removedtheorem strong_progress (t : Tm) : IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
465removed induction t with
466removed | c n => left; exact .const n
467removed | p t1 t2 ih1 ih2 =>
468removed right
469removed cases ih1 with
470removed | inl hv1 =>
471removed cases ih2 with
472removed | inl hv2 =>
473removed cases hv1 with
474removed | const n1 =>
475removed cases hv2 with
476removed | const n2 => exact ⟨.c (n1 + n2), .plus n1 n2⟩
477removed | inr h2 =>
478removed obtain ⟨t2', ht2⟩ := h2
479removed exact ⟨.p t1 t2', .plusRight t1 t2 t2' hv1 ht2⟩
480removed | inr h1 =>
481removed obtain ⟨t1', ht1⟩ := h1
482removed exact ⟨.p t1' t2, .plusLeft t1 t1' t2 ht1⟩
483removed
484removed-- This important property is called *strong progress*, because every term
485removed-- either is a value or can "make progress" by stepping to some other term.
486removed-- (The qualifier "strong" distinguishes it from a more refined version that
487removed-- we'll see in later chapters, called simply *progress*.)
488removed
489removed-- The idea of "making progress" can be extended to tell us something
490removed-- interesting about values in this language: they are exactly the terms that
491removed-- do *not* make progress in this sense. Let's give a name to "terms that
492removed-- cannot make progress." We'll call them *normal forms*.
493removed
494removeddef IsNormalForm {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t : X) : Prop :=
495removed ¬ ∃ t', R t t'
496removed
497removed-- Note that this definition specifies what it is to be a normal form for an
498removed-- *arbitrary* relation `R` over an arbitrary type `X`, not just for the
499removed-- particular single-step reduction relation over terms that we are interested
500removed-- in at the moment. We'll re-use the same terminology for talking about other
501removed-- relations later in the course.
502removed
503removed-- We can use this terminology to generalize the observation we made in the
504removed-- strong progress theorem: in this language (though not necessarily, in
505removed-- general), normal forms and values are actually the same thing.
506removed
507removedtheorem value_is_nf (v : Tm) (h : IsValue v) : IsNormalForm Step v := by
508removed intro hc
509removed obtain ⟨t', ht⟩ := hc
510removed cases h with
511removed | const n => cases ht
512removed
513removedtheorem nf_is_value (t : Tm) (h : IsNormalForm Step t) : IsValue t := by
514removed cases strong_progress t with
515removed | inl hv => exact hv
516removed | inr hstep => exact absurd hstep h
517removed
518removedtheorem nf_same_as_value (t : Tm) : IsNormalForm Step t ↔ IsValue t :=
519removed ⟨nf_is_value t, value_is_nf t⟩
520removed
521removed-- Why is this interesting? Because `IsValue` is a *syntactic* concept — it is
522removed-- defined by looking at the way a term is written — while `IsNormalForm` is a
523removed-- *semantic* one — it is defined by looking at how the term steps.
524removed
525removed-- It is not obvious that these concepts should characterize the same set of
526removed-- terms!
527removed
528removed-- Indeed, we could easily have written the definitions (incorrectly) so that
529removed-- they would *not* coincide.
530removed
531removed-- Suppose, for example, we define `IsValue` so that it includes some terms
532removed-- that are not finished reducing. (Even if you don't work the exercise
533removed-- `value_not_same_as_normal_form1` below and the following ones, make sure
534removed-- you can think of an example of such a term.)
535removed
536removednamespace Temp1
537removed
538removedinductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
539removed | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
540removed | funny (t1 : Tm) (n : Nat) : IsValue (.p t1 (.c n)) -- <---
541removed
542removedinductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
543removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
544removed | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : Step t1 t1') : Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
545removed | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : Step t2 t2') : Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
546removed
547removed-- _Quiz:_
548removed
549removed-- Using this wrong definition of `IsValue`, to how many different values does
550removed-- the following term reduce in zero or more steps?
551removed
552removed-- .p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 3)
553removed
554removed-- _Quiz:_
555removed
556removed-- To how many different terms does the following term `Step` (in one step)?
557removed
558removed-- .p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.p (.c 3) (.c 4))
559removed
560removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): value_not_same_as_normal_form1 ⭐⭐⭐
561removed
562removedtheorem value_not_same_as_normal_form :
563removed ∃ v, IsValue v ∧ ¬ IsNormalForm Step v := by
564removed apply Exists.intro (.p (.c 0) (.c 0))
565removed apply And.intro (.funny _ 0)
566removed sorry
567removed
568removedend Temp1
569removed
570removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): value_not_same_as_normal_form2 ⭐⭐
571removed
572removed-- Or we might (again, wrongly) define `Step` so that it permits something
573removed-- designated as a value to reduce further. We again lose the property that
574removed-- values are the same as normal forms.
575removed
576removednamespace Temp2
577removed
578removedinductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
579removed | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n) -- Original definition
580removed
581removedinductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
582removed | funny (n : Nat) : Step (.c n) (.p (.c n) (.c 0)) -- <--- NEW
583removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
584removed | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : Step t1 t1') : Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
585removed | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : Step t2 t2') : Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
586removed
587removed-- _Quiz:_
588removed
589removed-- With this definition, to how many different terms does the following term
590removed-- step (in exactly one step)?
591removed
592removed-- .p (.c 1) (.c 3)
593removed
594removedtheorem value_not_same_as_normal_form :
595removed ∃ v, IsValue v ∧ ¬ IsNormalForm Step v := by
596removed apply Exists.intro (.c 5)
597removed apply And.intro (.const 5)
598removed sorry
599removed
600removedend Temp2
601removed
602removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): value_not_same_as_normal_form3 ⭐⭐⭐
603removed
604removed-- Finally, we might define `IsValue` and `Step` so that there is some term
605removed-- that is *not* a value but that *also* cannot take a step. Such terms are
606removed-- said to be *stuck*. In this case, this is caused by a mistake in the
607removed-- semantics, but we will also see situations where, even in a correct
608removed-- language definition, it makes sense to allow some terms to be stuck. (Note
609removed-- that `plusRight` is missing below.)
610removed
611removednamespace Temp3
612removed
613removedinductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
614removed | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
615removed
616removedinductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
617removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
618removed | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : Step t1 t1') : Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
619removed
620removed-- _Quiz:_
621removed
622removed-- With this definition, to how many terms does the following term step (in
623removed-- one step)?
624removed
625removed-- .p (.c 1) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2))
626removed
627removedtheorem value_not_same_as_normal_form :
628removed ∃ t, ¬ IsValue t ∧ IsNormalForm Step t := by
629removed apply Exists.intro (.p (.c 1) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)))
630removed apply And.intro
631removed · sorry
632removed · sorry
633removed
634removedend Temp3
635removed
636removed-- ## Multi-Step Reduction
637removed
638removed-- We've been working so far with the *single-step reduction* relation `⟶`,
639removed-- which formalizes the individual steps of an abstract machine for executing
640removed-- programs. We can use the same machine to reduce programs to completion — to
641removed-- find out what final result they yield. This can be formalized as follows:
642removed
643removed-- - First, we define a *multi-step reduction relation* `⟶*`, which relates
644removed-- terms `t` and `t'` if `t` can reach `t'` by any number (including zero) of
645removed-- single reduction steps.
646removed
647removed-- - Then we define a "result" of a term `t` as a normal form that `t` can reach
648removed-- by multi-step reduction.
649removed
650removed-- Since we'll want to reuse the idea of multi-step reduction many times with
651removed-- many different single-step relations, let's define the concept generically.
652removed-- Given a relation `R` (e.g., the step relation `⟶`), we define a new
653removed-- relation `Multi R`, called the *multi-step closure of `R`*, as follows.
654removed
655removedinductive Multi {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : X → X → Prop where
656removed | refl (x : X) : Multi R x x
657removed | step (x y z : X) (h1 : R x y) (h2 : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z
658removed
659removed-- Note to developers (berberman):
660removed-- I would make some arguments implicit to proivde a cleaner interface
661removed-- (FYI the [mathlib
662removed-- version](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Logic/Relation.html#Relation.ReflTransGen))
663removed
664removed-- The effect of this definition is that `Multi R` relates two elements `x`
665removed-- and `y` if
666removed
667removed-- - `x = y`, or
668removed
669removed-- - `R x y`, or
670removed
671removed-- - there is some nonempty sequence `z₁`, `z₂` , ..., `zₙ` such that
672removed
673removed-- `R x₁ z₁,
674removed-- R z₁ z₂,
675removed-- ...,
676removed-- R zₙ y.`
677removed
678removed-- Intuitively, if `R` describes a single-step of computation, then
679removed-- `z₁ ... zₙ` are the intermediate steps of computation that get us from `x`
680removed-- to `y`.
681removed
682removed-- We write `⟶*` for the `Multi Step` relation on terms
683removed
684removednotation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
685removed
686removed-- The relation `Multi R` has several crucial properties.
687removed
688removed-- First, it is obviously *reflexive* (a term can execute to itself by taking
689removed-- zero steps). That is just what the `Multi.refl` constructor says, so such a
690removed-- goal can always be closed with `exact .refl _`. It comes up often enough
691removed-- that it is worth registering the constructor as a *reflexivity lemma*, with
692removed-- the `@[refl]` attribute. The `rfl` tactic then closes a zero-step execution
693removed-- exactly as it closes `x = x`:
694removed
695removedattribute [refl] Multi.refl
696removed
697removedexample : (.c 5 : Tm) ⟶* .c 5 := by rfl
698removed
699removed-- This pays off at the *end* of a reduction sequence too: the final
700removed-- `Multi.step` leaves a goal relating a term to itself, which `rfl`
701removed-- discharges.
702removed
703removedexample : (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) ⟶* .c (1 + 2) := by
704removed apply Multi.step (y := .c (1 + 2))
705removed · exact .plus 1 2
706removed · rfl
707removed
708removed-- Second, it *contains* `R` — single-step reductions are a particular case of
709removed-- multi-step executions. (It is this fact that justifies the word "closure"
710removed-- in "multi-step closure of `R`.")
711removed
712removedtheorem multi_single {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y : X) (h : R x y) :
713removed Multi R x y :=
714removed .step x y y h (.refl y)
715removed
716removed-- Third, `Multi R` is *transitive*.
717removed
718removedtheorem multi_trans {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y z : X)
719removed (g : Multi R x y) (h : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z := by
720removed induction g with
721removed | refl a => exact h
722removed | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact .step a b z h1 (ih h)
723removed
724removed-- In particular, for the `Multi Step` relation on terms, if `t1 ⟶* t2` and
725removed-- `t2 ⟶* t3`, then `t1 ⟶* t3`.
726removed
727removed-- _Quiz:_
728removed
729removed-- Which of the following relations on numbers *cannot* be expressed as
730removed-- `Multi R` for some `R`?
731removed
732removed-- (A) less than or equal (B) strictly less than (C) equal (D) none of the
733removed-- above
734removed
735removed-- ### Examples
736removed
737removedexample :
738removed (.p (.p (.c 0) (.c 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶* .c ((0 + 3) + (2 + 4)) := by
739removed apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4)))
740removed · exact .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 0 3)
741removed apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.c (2 + 4)))
742removed · exact .plusRight _ _ _ (.const _) (.plus 2 4)
743removed · exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus (0 + 3) (2 + 4))
744removed
745removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): test_multistep_2 ⭐
746removed
747removedexample : (.c 3 : Tm) ⟶* .c 3 := sorry
748removed
749removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): test_multistep_3 ⭐
750removed
751removedexample : (.p (.c 0) (.c 3)) ⟶* .p (.c 0) (.c 3) := sorry
752removed
753removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): test_multistep_4 ⭐⭐
754removed
755removedexample :
756removed (.p (.c 0) (.p (.c 2) (.p (.c 0) (.c 3))))
757removed ⟶* (.p (.c 0) (.c (2 + (0 + 3)))) := by
758removed sorry
759removed
760removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): test_multistep_rfl ⭐⭐
761removed
762removed-- Prove the following reduction, ending the chain with `rfl` instead of
763removed-- `multi_single`.
764removed
765removedexample : (.p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 4)) ⟶* .c ((1 + 2) + 4) := by
766removed sorry
767removed
768removed-- ### Normal Forms Again
769removed
770removed-- If `t` reduces to `t'` in zero or more steps and `t'` is a normal form, we
771removed-- say that "`t'` is *a normal form of* `t`."
772removed
773removeddef IsNormalFormOf {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t t' : X) : Prop :=
774removed Multi R t t' ∧ IsNormalForm R t'
775removed
776removed-- We have already seen that, for our language, single-step reduction is
777removed-- deterministic — i.e., a given term can take a single step in at most one
778removed-- way. It follows that, if `t` can reach a normal form, then this normal form
779removed-- is unique.
780removed
781removed-- In other words, we can actually pronounce `IsNormalFormOf t t'` as "`t'` is
782removed-- *the* normal form of `t`."
783removed
784removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): normal_forms_unique ⭐⭐⭐
785removed
786removedtheorem normal_forms_unique : Deterministic (IsNormalFormOf Step) := by
787removed -- We recommend using this initial setup as-is!
788removed intro x y1 y2 p1 p2
789removed obtain ⟨p11, p12⟩ := p1
790removed obtain ⟨p21, p22⟩ := p2
791removed sorry
792removed
793removed-- Indeed, something stronger is true for this language (though not for all
794removed-- the languages we will see): the reduction of *any* term `t` will eventually
795removed-- reach a normal form in a finite number of steps — i.e., `IsNormalFormOf` is
796removed-- a *total* function. We say the `Step` relation is *normalizing*. To prove
797removed-- it, we need a couple of congruence lemmas.
798removed
799removeddef Normalizing {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
800removed ∀ t, ∃ t', IsNormalFormOf R t t'
801removed
802removedtheorem multistep_congr_1 (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶* t1') : (.p t1 t2) ⟶* (.p t1' t2) := by
803removed induction h with
804removed | refl x => exact .refl _
805removed | step x y z h1 h2 ih => exact .step _ (.p y t2) _ (.plusLeft x y t2 h1) ih
806removed
807removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): multistep_congr_2 ⭐⭐
808removed
809removedtheorem multistep_congr_2 (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : t2 ⟶* t2') :
810removed (.p v1 t2) ⟶* (.p v1 t2') := by
811removed sorry
812removed
813removed-- With these lemmas in hand, the main proof is a straightforward induction.
814removed
815removed-- *Theorem*: The `Step` relation is normalizing — i.e., for every `t` there
816removed-- exists some `t'` such that `t` reduces to `t'` and `t'` is a normal form.
817removed
818removed-- *Proof sketch*: By induction on terms. There are two cases:
819removed
820removed-- - `t = c n` for some `n`. Here `t` doesn't take a step, and we have `t' = t`.
821removed-- We derive the left-hand side by reflexivity and the right-hand side by
822removed-- observing (a) that values are normal forms (by `nf_same_as_value`) and (b)
823removed-- that `t` is a value (by `const`).
824removed
825removed-- - `t = p t1 t2` for some `t1` and `t2`. By the IH, `t1` and `t2` reduce to
826removed-- normal forms `t1'` and `t2'`. Recall that normal forms are values (by
827removed-- `nf_same_as_value`); we therefore know that `t1' = c n1` and `t2' = c n2`
828removed-- for some `n1` and `n2`. We combine the `⟶*` derivations for `t1` and `t2`
829removed-- using `multistep_congr_1` and `multistep_congr_2` to prove that `p t1 t2`
830removed-- reduces in many steps to `t' = c (n1 + n2)`. Finally, `c (n1 + n2)` is a
831removed-- value, which is in turn a normal form.
832removed
833removedtheorem step_normalizing : Normalizing Step := by
834removed intro t
835removed induction t with
836removed | c n => exact ⟨.c n, .refl _, (nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const n)⟩
837removed | p t1 t2 ih1 ih2 =>
838removed obtain ⟨t1', hs1, hnf1⟩ := ih1
839removed obtain ⟨t2', hs2, hnf2⟩ := ih2
840removed obtain ⟨n1⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf1
841removed obtain ⟨n2⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf2
842removed apply Exists.intro (.c (n1 + n2))
843removed apply And.intro _ ((nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const _))
844removed apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_1 t1 (.c n1) t2 hs1)
845removed apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_2 (.c n1) t2 (.c n2) (.const n1) hs2)
846removed exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus n1 n2)
847removed
848removed-- ### Equivalence of Big-Step and Small-Step
849removed
850removed-- Having defined the operational semantics of our tiny programming language
851removed-- in two different ways (big-step and small-step), it makes sense to ask
852removed-- whether these definitions actually define the same thing!
853removed
854removed-- They do, though it takes a little work to show it. The details are left as
855removed-- an exercise. We consider the two implications separately. First, big-step
856removed-- evaluation implies multi-step reduction to a value.
857removed
858removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval ⭐⭐⭐
859removed
860removedtheorem multistep_of_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) (h : t ⇓ n) : t ⟶* .c n := by
861removed sorry
862removed
863removed-- The key ideas in the proof can be seen in the following picture:
864removed
865removed-- p t1 t2 ⟶ (by plusLeft)
866removed-- p t1' t2 ⟶ (by plusLeft)
867removed-- p t1'' t2 ⟶ (by plusLeft)
868removed-- ...
869removed-- p (c n1) t2 ⟶ (by plusRight)
870removed-- p (c n1) t2' ⟶ (by plusRight)
871removed-- p (c n1) t2'' ⟶ (by plusRight)
872removed-- ...
873removed-- p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶ (by plus)
874removed-- c (n1 + n2)
875removed
876removed-- That is, the multi-step reduction of a term of the form `p t1 t2` proceeds
877removed-- in three phases:
878removed
879removed-- - First, we use `plusLeft` some number of times to reduce `t1` to a normal
880removed-- form, which must (by `nf_same_as_value`) be a term of the form `c n1` for
881removed-- some `n1`.
882removed
883removed-- - Next, we use `plusRight` some number of times to reduce `t2` to a normal
884removed-- form, which must again be a term of the form `c n2` for some `n2`.
885removed
886removed-- - Finally, we use `plus` one time to reduce `p (c n1) (c n2)` to
887removed-- `c (n1 + n2)`.
888removed
889removed-- To formalize this intuition, you'll need the congruence lemmas from above,
890removed-- plus some basic properties of `⟶*` (that it is reflexive, transitive, and
891removed-- includes `⟶`).
892removed
893removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval_inf ⭐⭐⭐
894removed
895removed-- Write a detailed informal version of the proof of `multistep_of_eval`. (A
896removed-- paper exercise — there is no Lean proof to fill in here.)
897removed
898removed-- For the converse, we need one lemma, which establishes a relation between
899removed-- single-step reduction and big-step evaluation. A single step preserves the
900removed-- big-step value.
901removed
902removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): eval_of_step ⭐⭐⭐
903removed
904removedtheorem eval_of_step (t t' : Tm) (n : Nat) (hs : t ⟶ t') (he : t' ⇓ n) : t ⇓ n := by
905removed sorry
906removed
907removed-- The fact that small-step reduction implies big-step evaluation is now
908removed-- straightforward to prove, once we have factored out the observation that
909removed-- every normal form is a value. The proof proceeds by induction on the
910removed-- multi-step reduction sequence that is buried in the hypothesis
911removed-- `IsNormalFormOf t t'`. (Make sure you understand the statement before you
912removed-- start to work on the proof.)
913removed
914removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): eval_of_multistep ⭐⭐⭐
915removed
916removedtheorem eval_of_multistep (t t' : Tm) (h : IsNormalFormOf Step t t') :
917removed ∃ n, t' = .c n ∧ t ⇓ n := by
918removed sorry
919removed
920removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): interp_tm ⭐⭐⭐
921removed
922removed-- Remember that we also defined big-step evaluation of terms as a function
923removed-- `evalF`. Prove that it is equivalent to the relational semantics. (Hint: we
924removed-- just proved that `Eval` and `multistep` are equivalent, so logically it
925removed-- doesn't matter which you choose. One will be easier than the other,
926removed-- though!)
927removed
928removedtheorem evalF_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) : evalF t = n ↔ t ⇓ n := by
929removed sorry
930removed
931removed-- ## Small-Step Slang
932removed
933removed-- Now for a more serious example: a small-step semantics for the richer
934removed-- arithmetic and boolean expressions of the Slang chapter (with subtraction,
935removed-- multiplication, and the boolean operators) rather than the two-constructor
936removed-- toy language we have used so far.
937removed
938removed-- The small-step reduction relations for these expressions are
939removed-- straightforward extensions of the tiny language we've been working up to
940removed-- now. To make them easier to read, we introduce the symbolic notations `⟶a`
941removed-- and `⟶b` for the arithmetic and boolean step relations.
942removed
943removed-- We work in the `Slang` namespace, reusing the arithmetic and boolean
944removed-- expression syntax (`Aexp`, `Bexp`) and the big-step evaluator (`Aexp.eval`)
945removed-- from the `Slang` chapter:
946removed
947removednamespace Slang
948removed
949removed-- ### Arithmetic Expressions
950removed
951removed-- The arithmetic *values* (the normal forms of the small-step relation below)
952removed-- are just the numeric literals:
953removed
954removedinductive IsAValue : Aexp → Prop where
955removed | num (n : Nat) : IsAValue (.num n)
956removed
957removed-- Here is the small-step relation for arithmetic expressions. A compound
958removed-- expression reduces its left operand first; once that is a value, it reduces
959removed-- its right operand; once both are values, it computes the result. (We show
960removed-- the rules for `+` in full; those for `−` and `×` have exactly the same
961removed-- shape.)
962removed
963removed-- a1 ⟶a a1'
964removed-- -------------------- (plusLeft)
965removed-- a1 + a2 ⟶a a1' + a2
966removed
967removed-- IsAValue v1 a2 ⟶a a2'
968removed-- --------------------------- (plusRight)
969removed-- v1 + a2 ⟶a v1 + a2'
970removed
971removed-- ------------------------- (plus)
972removed-- n1 + n2 ⟶a num (n1 + n2)
973removed
974removedinductive AStep : Aexp → Aexp → Prop where
975removed | plusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1' a2)
976removed | plusRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
977removed AStep (.plus v1 a2) (.plus v1 a2')
978removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.plus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 + n2))
979removed | minusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1' a2)
980removed | minusRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
981removed AStep (.minus v1 a2) (.minus v1 a2')
982removed | minus (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.minus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 - n2))
983removed | multLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1' a2)
984removed | multRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
985removed AStep (.mult v1 a2) (.mult v1 a2')
986removed | mult (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.mult (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 * n2))
987removed
988removedscoped notation:40 a:41 " ⟶a " a':41 => AStep a a'
989removed
990removed-- Notice that `AStep` has exactly the shape `Aexp → Aexp → Prop` — i.e., it
991removed-- is a `Relation Aexp` in the sense of the *Relations* section above. So the
992removed-- generic vocabulary from that section (`Deterministic`, `IsNormalForm`, the
993removed-- multi-step closure `Multi`, ...) applies to it directly.
994removed
995removed-- Here is a one-step reduction: since the left operand `3` is already a
996removed-- value, the right operand is the one that takes a step.
997removed
998removedexample :
999removed (Aexp.plus (.num 3) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 1))) ⟶a (.plus (.num 3) (.num 3)) :=
1000removed .plusRight _ _ _ (.num 3) (.plus 2 1)
1001removed
1002removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): strong_progress_arith ⭐⭐
1003removed
1004removed-- Every arithmetic expression is either a value or can take a step — the same
1005removed-- *strong progress* property we proved for the toy language, now for the
1006removed-- richer `Slang` arithmetic expressions.
1007removed
1008removedtheorem strong_progress_arith (a : Aexp) : IsAValue a ∨ ∃ a', a ⟶a a' := by
1009removed sorry
1010removed
1011removed-- ### Boolean Expressions
1012removed
1013removed-- The small-step relation for boolean expressions reduces the arithmetic
1014removed-- subexpressions of a comparison (using `⟶a`) and then applies the
1015removed-- comparison, and it short-circuits `¬` and `∧` on boolean literals.
1016removed
1017removed-- We are not actually going to bother to define boolean values, since they
1018removed-- aren't needed in the definition of `⟶b` below (why?), though they might be
1019removed-- if our language were a bit more complicated (why?).
1020removed
1021removed-- Again we show a representative sample; `neq`, `le`, and `gt` follow the
1022removed-- same pattern as `eq`.
1023removed
1024removed-- a1 ⟶a a1'
1025removed-- -------------------- (eqLeft)
1026removed-- a1 = a2 ⟶b a1' = a2
1027removed
1028removed-- IsAValue v1 a2 ⟶a a2'
1029removed-- --------------------------- (eqRight)
1030removed-- v1 = a2 ⟶b v1 = a2'
1031removed
1032removed-- --------------------- (eq)
1033removed-- n1 = n2 ⟶b (n1 = n2)
1034removed
1035removed-- b1 ⟶b b1'
1036removed-- -------------- (notStep)
1037removed-- ¬ b1 ⟶b ¬ b1'
1038removed
1039removed-- ---------------- (notTrue)
1040removed-- ¬ true ⟶b false
1041removed
1042removed-- --------------------- (andFalse)
1043removed-- false ∧ b2 ⟶b false
1044removed
1045removed-- Here are the formal rules.
1046removed
1047removedinductive BStep : Bexp → Bexp → Prop where
1048removed | eqLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.eq a1 a2) (.eq a1' a2)
1049removed | eqRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1050removed BStep (.eq v1 a2) (.eq v1 a2')
1051removed | eq (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.eq (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 = n2)))
1052removed | neqLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.neq a1 a2) (.neq a1' a2)
1053removed | neqRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1054removed BStep (.neq v1 a2) (.neq v1 a2')
1055removed | neq (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.neq (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 ≠ n2)))
1056removed | leLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.le a1 a2) (.le a1' a2)
1057removed | leRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1058removed BStep (.le v1 a2) (.le v1 a2')
1059removed | le (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.le (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 ≤ n2)))
1060removed | gtLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.gt a1 a2) (.gt a1' a2)
1061removed | gtRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1062removed BStep (.gt v1 a2) (.gt v1 a2')
1063removed | gt (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.gt (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 > n2)))
1064removed | notStep (b1 b1' : Bexp) (h : BStep b1 b1') : BStep (.not b1) (.not b1')
1065removed | notTrue : BStep (.not (.bool true)) (.bool false)
1066removed | notFalse : BStep (.not (.bool false)) (.bool true)
1067removed | andStep (b1 b1' b2 : Bexp) (h : BStep b1 b1') : BStep (.and b1 b2) (.and b1' b2)
1068removed | andTrueStep (b2 b2' : Bexp) (h : BStep b2 b2') :
1069removed BStep (.and (.bool true) b2) (.and (.bool true) b2')
1070removed | andFalse (b2 : Bexp) : BStep (.and (.bool false) b2) (.bool false)
1071removed | andTrueTrue : BStep (.and (.bool true) (.bool true)) (.bool true)
1072removed | andTrueFalse : BStep (.and (.bool true) (.bool false)) (.bool false)
1073removed
1074removedscoped notation:40 b:41 " ⟶b " b':41 => BStep b b'
1075removed
1076removed-- A boolean example — the left comparison operand reduces first:
1077removed
1078removedexample :
1079removed (Bexp.le (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.num 3)) ⟶b (.le (.num 2) (.num 3)) :=
1080removed .leLeft _ _ _ (.plus 1 1)
1081removed
1082removed-- _Quiz:_
1083removed
1084removed-- Which of these properties does this small-step semantics for `Slang`
1085removed-- expressions satisfy? (Yes or No for each.)
1086removed
1087removed-- - determinism
1088removed-- - strong progress (every non-value takes a step)
1089removed-- - values and normal forms coincide (i.e., there are no "stuck" terms)
1090removed-- - the step relation is normalizing (i.e., evaluation always terminates)
1091removed
1092removed-- Let us make good on the first of those answers. Both step relations are
1093removed-- *deterministic*: the value guards on the "step the right operand" rules
1094removed-- mean that at most one rule ever applies to a given term.
1095removed
1096removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
1097removed
1098removed-- The arithmetic step relation is deterministic. (Structurally this is the
1099removed-- value-based determinism proof from the toy language, repeated for `+`, `−`,
1100removed-- and `×`; the impossible cross-cases close because a value `num n` cannot
1101removed-- step.)
1102removed
1103removedtheorem astep_deterministic : Deterministic AStep := by
1104removed sorry
1105removed
1106removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): bstep_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
1107removed
1108removed-- The boolean step relation is deterministic too. The comparison cases (`eq`,
1109removed-- `neq`, `le`, `gt`) reduce their operands with `⟶a`, so they inherit
1110removed-- determinism from `astep_deterministic`; `¬` and the short-circuiting `∧`
1111removed-- contribute only base cases.
1112removed
1113removedtheorem bstep_deterministic : Deterministic BStep := by
1114removed sorry
1115removed
1116removed-- ### Nondeterministic Evaluation
1117removed
1118removed-- The relation `⟶a` above bakes in a *left-to-right* evaluation order: the
1119removed-- rule `plusRight` can fire only once the left operand is already a value
1120removed-- (`IsAValue v1`). But nothing about the *meaning* of `+` requires that order
1121removed-- — we could just as well reduce the right operand first, or interleave the
1122removed-- two. Different orders are exactly what a concurrent or optimizing
1123removed-- implementation might choose, so it is natural to ask whether the choice can
1124removed-- affect the final answer.
1125removed
1126removed-- Let's find out. We define a second small-step relation, `⟶n`, that is
1127removed-- identical to `⟶a` except that we *drop* the `IsAValue` side-condition:
1128removed-- either operand may take a step at any time.
1129removed
1130removedinductive ANStep : Aexp → Aexp → Prop where
1131removed | plusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1' a2)
1132removed | plusRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1 a2')
1133removed | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.plus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 + n2))
1134removed | minusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1' a2)
1135removed | minusRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1 a2')
1136removed | minus (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.minus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 - n2))
1137removed | multLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1' a2)
1138removed | multRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1 a2')
1139removed | mult (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.mult (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 * n2))
1140removed
1141removedscoped notation:40 a:41 " ⟶n " a':41 => ANStep a a'
1142removed
1143removed-- Unlike `⟶a`, this relation really is nondeterministic: a single term can
1144removed-- step in two different ways, depending on which operand we choose to
1145removed-- advance.
1146removed
1147removedtheorem anstep_not_deterministic : ¬ Deterministic ANStep := by
1148removed intro hd
1149removed have s1 : ANStep (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)))
1150removed (.plus (.num 2) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2))) :=
1151removed .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 1 1)
1152removed have s2 : ANStep (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)))
1153removed (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.num 4)) :=
1154removed .plusRight _ _ _ (.plus 2 2)
1155removed have heq := hd _ _ _ s1 s2
1156removed simp at heq
1157removed
1158removed-- Remarkably, this nondeterminism does *not* affect the final answer. The key
1159removed-- observation is that a single step never changes the big-step *value* of an
1160removed-- expression — whichever operand we advance, `eval` is preserved.
1161removed
1162removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): anstep_preserves_eval ⭐⭐
1163removed
1164removed-- Prove that one nondeterministic step leaves the big-step value unchanged.
1165removed-- *Hint:* induction on the step derivation; each case is immediate from
1166removed-- `eval` and, where present, the induction hypothesis.
1167removed
1168removedtheorem anstep_preserves_eval (a a' : Aexp) (h : a ⟶n a') : a.eval = a'.eval := by
1169removed sorry
1170removed
1171removed-- This lifts to any number of steps by a routine induction on the multi-step
1172removed-- derivation:
1173removed
1174removedtheorem multi_anstep_preserves_eval (a a' : Aexp) (h : Multi ANStep a a') : a.eval = a'.eval := by
1175removed induction h with
1176removed | refl x => rfl
1177removed | step x y z h1 _ ih => rw [anstep_preserves_eval x y h1]; exact ih
1178removed
1179removed-- Finally we can compare the two semantics. The deterministic relation `⟶a`
1180removed-- is a *special case* of `⟶n`: every `⟶a` step is also an `⟶n` step (it
1181removed-- merely happens, in addition, to respect the `IsAValue` guard).
1182removed
1183removedtheorem astep_imp_anstep (a a' : Aexp) (h : a ⟶a a') : a ⟶n a' := by
1184removed induction h with
1185removed | plusLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .plusLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
1186removed | plusRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .plusRight v1 a2 a2' ih
1187removed | plus n1 n2 => exact .plus n1 n2
1188removed | minusLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .minusLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
1189removed | minusRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .minusRight v1 a2 a2' ih
1190removed | minus n1 n2 => exact .minus n1 n2
1191removed | multLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .multLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
1192removed | multRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .multRight v1 a2 a2' ih
1193removed | mult n1 n2 => exact .mult n1 n2
1194removed
1195removedtheorem multi_astep_imp_anstep (a a' : Aexp) (h : Multi AStep a a') : Multi ANStep a a' := by
1196removed induction h with
1197removed | refl x => exact .refl x
1198removed | step x y z h1 _ ih => exact .step x y z (astep_imp_anstep x y h1) ih
1199removed
1200removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_anstep_agree ⭐⭐⭐
1201removed
1202removed-- Now put the pieces together: prove that the deterministic and
1203removed-- nondeterministic semantics always compute the *same* final result. That is,
1204removed-- if `a` fully reduces to `.num n1` under `⟶a` and to `.num n2` under `⟶n`,
1205removed-- then `n1 = n2`.
1206removed
1207removed-- *Hint:* both `.num n1` and `.num n2` are reachable by `⟶n` (use
1208removed-- `multi_astep_imp_anstep` for the first), and `⟶n` preserves `eval`.
1209removed
1210removedtheorem astep_anstep_agree (a : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat)
1211removed (hd : Multi AStep a (.num n1)) (hn : Multi ANStep a (.num n2)) : n1 = n2 := by
1212removed sorry
1213removed
1214removed-- So even though `⟶n` is genuinely nondeterministic, the value it eventually
1215removed-- produces is completely determined — and it is the same value the
1216removed-- deterministic machine (and the big-step evaluator) computes. This
1217removed-- *confluence to a unique result* is exactly the property one wants when
1218removed-- reordering or parallelizing the evaluation of pure expressions.
1219removed
1220removed-- ### A Small-Step Stack Machine
1221removed
1222removed-- Our last example is a small-step semantics for a *stack machine* that
1223removed-- evaluates arithmetic expressions. The machine's instructions push a
1224removed-- constant or combine the top two stack entries. The machine's behavior
1225removed-- should match the big-step `Aexp.eval` function defined earlier.
1226removed
1227removed-- A *program* is a list of instructions, and the *stack* is a list of
1228removed-- numbers.
1229removed
1230removedinductive SInstr where
1231removed | push (n : Nat)
1232removed | plus
1233removed | minus
1234removed | mult
1235removed
1236removedabbrev Stack := List Nat
1237removedabbrev Prog := List SInstr
1238removed
1239removed-- The compiler emits code in the postfix order sketched above:
1240removed
1241removeddef compile : Aexp → Prog
1242removed | .num n => [.push n]
1243removed | .plus a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.plus]
1244removed | .minus a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.minus]
1245removed | .mult a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.mult]
1246removed
1247removedexample : compile (.plus (.num 2) (.num 3)) = [.push 2, .push 3, .plus] := rfl
1248removed
1249removed-- Now the small-step machine itself: each step consumes the next instruction
1250removed-- and updates the stack.
1251removed
1252removedinductive StackStep : Prog × Stack → Prog × Stack → Prop where
1253removed | push (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n : Nat) : StackStep (.push n :: p, stk) (p, n :: stk)
1254removed | plus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1255removed StackStep (.plus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m + n) :: stk)
1256removed | minus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1257removed StackStep (.minus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m - n) :: stk)
1258removed | mult (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1259removed StackStep (.mult :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m * n) :: stk)
1260removed
1261removed-- The machine is deterministic:
1262removed
1263removedtheorem stack_step_deterministic : Deterministic StackStep := by
1264removed intro x y1 y2 h1 h2
1265removed cases h1 <;> cases h2 <;> rfl
1266removed
1267removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): compiler_is_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1268removed
1269removed-- Prove the compiler correct: running the compiled program from the empty
1270removed-- stack reduces, in some number of steps, to a stack holding exactly the
1271removed-- value of the expression.
1272removed
1273removed-- *Hint:* this will not go through by a direct induction — the induction
1274removed-- hypothesis is too weak. Prove a more general statement first, about running
1275removed-- `compile a` followed by *any* leftover program `p`, starting from *any*
1276removed-- stack `stk`. (Reassociating the `++`s with `List.append_assoc`, and
1277removed-- chaining steps with `multi_trans`/`multi_single`, are the moves you need.)
1278removed
1279removedtheorem compiler_is_correct (a : Aexp) :
1280removed Multi StackStep (compile a, []) ([], [a.eval]) := by
1281removed sorry
1282removed
1283removedend Slang
1284removed
