7removed
8removed-- # Stlc: The Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
9removed
10removed-- The simply typed lambda-calculus (STLC) is a tiny core calculus embodying
11removed-- the key concept of *functional abstraction*. This concept shows up in
12removed-- pretty much every real-world programming language in some form (functions,
13removed-- procedures, methods, etc.).
14removed
15removed-- We will follow exactly the same pattern as in the previous chapter when
16removed-- formalizing this calculus (syntax, small-step semantics, typing rules) and
17removed-- its main properties (progress and preservation). The new technical
18removed-- challenges arise from the mechanisms of *variable binding* and
19removed-- *substitution*. It will take some work to deal with these.
20removed
21removed-- The STLC lives in the lower-left front corner of the famous *lambda cube*
22removed-- (also called the *Barendregt Cube*), which visualizes three sets of
23removed-- features that can be added to its simple core:
24removed
25removed-- Calculus of Constructions
26removed-- type operators +--------+
27removed-- /| /|
28removed-- / | / |
29removed-- polymorphism +--------+ |
30removed-- | | | |
31removed-- | +-----|--+
32removed-- | / | /
33removed-- |/ |/
34removed-- +--------+ dependent types
35removed-- STLC
36removed
37removed-- Moving from bottom to top in the cube corresponds to adding *polymorphic
38removed-- types* like `∀ α : Type, α → α`. Adding *just* polymorphism gives us the
39removed-- famous Girard-Reynolds calculus, System F.
40removed
41removed-- Moving from front to back corresponds to adding *type operators* like
42removed-- `List`.
43removed
44removed-- Moving from left to right corresponds to adding *dependent types* like
45removed-- `∀ n, ArrayOfSize n`.
46removed
47removed-- The top right corner on the back, which combines all three features, is
48removed-- called the *Calculus of Constructions*. First studied by Coquand and Huet,
49removed-- it forms the foundation of Lean's logic.
50removed
51removed-- ## Overview
52removed
53removed-- The STLC is built on some collection of *base types*: booleans, numbers,
54removed-- strings, etc. The exact choice of base types doesn't matter much — the
55removed-- definition of the language as well as its theoretical properties work out
56removed-- the same no matter what we choose — so for the sake of brevity let's take
57removed-- just `Bool` for the moment. In the next chapter we'll see how to add more
58removed-- base types, and in later chapters we'll enrich the pure STLC with other
59removed-- useful constructs like pairs, records, subtyping, and mutable state.
60removed
61removed-- Starting from boolean constants and conditionals, we add three things:
62removed
63removed-- - variables
64removed-- - function abstractions
65removed-- - application
66removed
67removed-- This gives us the following collection of abstract syntax constructors
68removed-- (written out first in informal BNF notation — we'll formalize it below) for
69removed-- STLC terms `t`.
70removed
71removed-- t ::= x (variable)
72removed-- | λ x : T . t (abstraction)
73removed-- | t t (application)
74removed-- | true (constant true)
75removed-- | false (constant false)
76removed-- | if t then t else t (conditional)
77removed
78removed-- The Greek letter λ ("lambda") in a function abstraction `λx:T. t` is what
79removed-- gives the calculus its name. The variable `x` is called the *parameter* to
80removed-- the function; the term `t` is its *body*. The annotation `:T` specifies the
81removed-- *type* of arguments that the function can be applied to.
82removed
83removed-- The types of the STLC include `Bool`, which classifies the boolean
84removed-- constants `true` and `false` as well as more complex computations that
85removed-- yield booleans, plus *arrow types* that classify functions (as is the case
86removed-- in Lean).
87removed
88removed-- T ::= Bool
89removed-- | T → T
90removed
91removed-- Some examples of STLC terms:
92removed
93removed-- `λx:Bool. x`
94removed
95removed-- The identity function for booleans.
96removed
97removed-- `(λx:Bool. x) true`
98removed
99removed-- The identity function for booleans, applied to the boolean `true`.
100removed
101removed-- `λx:Bool. if x then false else true`
102removed
103removed-- The boolean "not" function.
104removed
105removed-- `λx:Bool. true`
106removed
107removed-- The constant function that takes every (boolean) argument to `true`.
108removed
109removed-- `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x`
110removed
111removed-- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first one.
112removed
113removed-- (As in Lean, a two-argument function in the lambda-calculus is really a
114removed-- one-argument function whose body is also a one-argument function.)
115removed
116removed-- `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true`
117removed
118removed-- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first one,
119removed-- applied to the booleans `false` and `true`.
120removed
121removed-- (As in Lean, application associates to the left — i.e., this expression is
122removed-- parsed as `((λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false) true`.)
123removed
124removed-- `λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)`
125removed
126removed-- A higher-order function that takes a *function* `f` (from booleans to
127removed-- booleans) as an argument, applies `f` to `true`, and applies `f` again to
128removed-- the result.
129removed
130removed-- `(λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)`
131removed
132removed-- The same higher-order function, applied to the constantly `false` function.
133removed
134removed-- The last two examples show, the STLC is a language of *higher-order*
135removed-- functions: we can write down functions that take other functions as
136removed-- arguments and/or return other functions as results.
137removed
138removed-- The STLC doesn't provide any primitive syntax for defining *named*
139removed-- functions: i.e., all functions are "anonymous." We'll see in chapter
140removed-- `MoreStlc` that it is easy to add named functions — indeed, the fundamental
141removed-- naming and binding mechanisms are exactly the same.
142removed
143removed-- Now reconsider our examples, each along with its type:
144removed
145removed-- - `λx:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool`
146removed
147removed-- - `(λx:Bool. x) true` has type `Bool`
148removed
149removed-- - `λx:Bool. if x then false else true` has type `Bool → Bool`
150removed
151removed-- - `λx:Bool. true` has type `Bool → Bool`
152removed
153removed-- - `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool → Bool` (i.e.,
154removed-- `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`)
155removed
156removed-- - `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true` has type `Bool`
157removed
158removed-- The last two, higher-order examples are left off the list on purpose —
159removed-- working out their types is the subject of the quizzes that follow.
160removed
161removed-- _Quiz:_
162removed
163removed-- What is the type of the following term?
164removed
165removed-- λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)
166removed
167removed-- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
168removed
169removed-- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
170removed
171removed-- (C) `Bool → Bool`
172removed
173removed-- (D) `Bool`
174removed
175removed-- (E) none of the above
176removed
177removed-- _Quiz:_
178removed
179removed-- How about the type of this one?
180removed
181removed-- (λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)
182removed
183removed-- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
184removed
185removed-- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
186removed
187removed-- (C) `Bool → Bool`
188removed
189removed-- (D) `Bool`
190removed
191removed-- (E) none of the above
192removed
193removed-- ## Syntax
194removed
195removed-- We next formalize the syntax of the STLC.
196removed
197removednamespace Stlc
198removed
199removedopen scoped MyGetElem
200removed
201removed-- ### Types
202removed
203removedinductive Ty where
204removed | bool
205removed | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
206removed
207removed-- ### Terms
208removed
209removedinductive Tm where
210removed | var (x : String)
211removed | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
212removed | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
213removed | tru
214removed | fls
215removed | ite (c t e : Tm)
216removed
217removed-- We need some notation magic to set up the concrete syntax, as we did in the
218removed-- Types chapter...
219removed
220removed-- The upshot of this section is that STLC types and terms are both written
221removed-- inside one pair of brackets, `<{ … }>`, and that `~e` inside the brackets
222removed-- escapes back to an arbitrary Lean expression:
223removed
224removed-- - `<{ Bool → Bool }>` is a type;
225removed
226removed-- - `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` is a term — a bare identifier inside the brackets is
227removed-- the object-language variable of that name, so `<{ x }>` is the variable
228removed-- `x`;
229removed
230removed-- - `<{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>` applies one Lean-level term to another.
231removed
232removed-- Lean works out from context which of the two a given bracket holds, so the
233removed-- same brackets serve for types, for terms, and — when we come to typing —
234removed-- for typing judgments too. How that works is in the collapsed blocks below;
235removed-- nothing later in the chapter depends on it.
236removed
237removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: types
238removed
239removed-- The `stlcTy` grammar covers `Bool`, arrows (written `→` or `->`,
240removed-- associating to the right), parentheses, and `~e`. A bare identifier other
241removed-- than `Bool` is spliced in as a Lean term, so a local `T` — or any Lean
242removed-- expression of type `Ty` — can appear directly inside the brackets.
243removed
244removed-- To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax` line to the category
245removed-- and a matching `macro_rules` case; that is all it takes to add a new type
246removed-- construct.
247removed
248removeddeclare_syntax_cat stlcTy
249removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTy
250removedsyntax:max "(" stlcTy ")" : stlcTy
251removedsyntax:max ident : stlcTy
252removedsyntax:50 stlcTy:51 " → " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
253removedsyntax:50 stlcTy:51 " -> " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
254removedsyntax:max (name := tyBracket) "<{ " stlcTy " }>" : term
255removed
256removedmacro_rules (kind := tyBracket)
257removed | `(<{ ~$T:term }>) => pure T
258removed | `(<{ ($T:stlcTy) }>) => `(<{ $T:stlcTy }>)
259removed | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
260removed match x.getId.toString with
261removed | "Bool" => `(Ty.bool)
262removed | _ => `(($x : Ty))
263removed | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy → $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
264removed | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy -> $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
265removed
266removed-- We'll write types inside of `<{ ... }>` brackets:
267removed
268removed#check <{ Bool }>
269removed#check <{ Bool -> Bool }>
270removed#check <{ (Bool -> Bool) -> Bool }>
271removed
272removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: terms
273removed
274removed-- Terms are built from variables, application (associating to the left),
275removed-- abstraction, the two boolean constants, and conditionals. A binding
276removed-- occurrence — the `x` in `λ x : T . t` — has a small grammar of its own,
277removed-- `stlcVar`, and `varStr` turns it into the string that `Tm.abs` stores.
278removed
279removed-- Because types and terms share the brackets, each `macro_rules` group says
280removed-- which bracket it belongs to (`kind := tyBracket`, `kind := tmBracket`), and
281removed-- each antiquote in a nested quotation says which grammar it came from. A
282removed-- bare identifier is the one genuinely overlapping case: `Bool` in term
283removed-- position would otherwise quietly become a variable named `Bool`, so that
284removed-- rule rejects it, which also settles which grammar a lone `<{ Bool }>`
285removed-- belongs to.
286removed
287removed-- The last production, `[x := s] t`, is the notation for substitution; we
288removed-- give it its meaning when we define substitution below. It binds tighter
289removed-- than application, so `[x:=s] t₁ t₂` is the application of `[x:=s] t₁` to
290removed-- `t₂`, and a `λ` or `if` body must be parenthesized:
291removed-- `[x:=s] (λ y : Bool . x)`.
292removed
293removeddeclare_syntax_cat stlcVar
294removedsyntax:max ident : stlcVar
295removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : stlcVar
296removed
297removedopen Lean in
298removed/-- The string named by a variable in binding position. -/
299removeddef varStr (x : TSyntax `stlcVar) : MacroM Term :=
300removed match x with
301removed | `(stlcVar| $i:ident) => pure (quote i.getId.toString : Term)
302removed | `(stlcVar| ~$e) => pure e
303removed | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
304removed
305removeddeclare_syntax_cat stlcTm
306removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTm
307removedsyntax:max "(" stlcTm ")" : stlcTm
308removedsyntax:max ident : stlcTm
309removedsyntax:75 stlcTm:75 ppSpace stlcTm:76 : stlcTm
310removedsyntax:50 "λ " stlcVar " : " stlcTy " . " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
311removedsyntax:50 "if " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
312removedsyntax:max "[" stlcVar " := " stlcTm "] " stlcTm:max : stlcTm
313removedsyntax:max (name := tmBracket) "<{ " stlcTm " }>" : term
314removed
315removedopen Lean in
316removedmacro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
317removed | `(<{ ~$e:term }>) => pure e
318removed | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
319removed | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
320removed match x.getId.toString with
321removed | "true" => `(Tm.tru)
322removed | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
323removed | "Bool" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Bool` is a type, not a term"
324removed | _ => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
325removed | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
326removed | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
327removed `(Tm.abs $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
328removed | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) =>
329removed `(Tm.ite <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)
330removed
331removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing it back
332removed
333removed-- A *delaborator* runs the grammar backwards: it rebuilds the concrete syntax
334removed-- from a `Ty` or `Tm` value, so that types and terms appearing in goals and
335removed-- in `#check` output print as `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` rather than as a pile of
336removed-- constructors. (Setting `pp.notation false` turns it off, revealing the
337removed-- underlying representation.)
338removed
339removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
340removed/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTy` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
341removed@[category_parenthesizer stlcTy]
342removeddef stlcTy.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
343removed maybeParenthesize `stlcTy true wrapParens prec <|
344removed parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTy prec
345removedwhere
346removed wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
347removed let pstx ← `(stlcTy| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
348removed return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
349removed
350removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
351removed/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
352removed@[category_parenthesizer stlcTm]
353removeddef stlcTm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
354removed maybeParenthesize `stlcTm true wrapParens prec <|
355removed parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTm prec
356removedwhere
357removed wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
358removed let pstx ← `(stlcTm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
359removed return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
360removed
361removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
362removed/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
363removedpartial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
364removed let stx ←
365removed match_expr ← getExpr with
366removed | Ty.bool => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
367removed | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
368removed let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
369removed let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
370removed `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
371removed | _ => do
372removed match ← delab with
373removed | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
374removed | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
375removed (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
376removed
377removedopen Lean in
378removed/-- Is `s` usable as a bare identifier in the object syntax? -/
379removeddef isPlainName (s : String) : Bool :=
380removed !s.isEmpty && s != "_" && !s.front.isDigit &&
381removed s.all fun c => c.isAlphanum || c == '_'
382removed
383removedopen Lean in
384removed/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
385removeddef isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
386removed isPlainName s && s != "true" && s != "false" && s != "Bool"
387removed
388removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
389removed/-- Rebuild `stlcVar` concrete syntax from the string in a binding position. -/
390removeddef delabVarInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcVar) := do
391removed match ← delab with
392removed | `($s:str) =>
393removed if isPlainName s.getString then
394removed `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
395removed else `(stlcVar| ~$s)
396removed | e => `(stlcVar| ~$e)
397removed
398removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
399removed/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
400removedpartial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
401removed let stx ←
402removed match_expr ← getExpr with
403removed | Tm.tru => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
404removed | Tm.fls => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
405removed | Tm.var _ => do
406removed let x ← withAppArg delab
407removed match x with
408removed | `($s:str) =>
409removed if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
410removed `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
411removed else
412removed let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
413removed `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
414removed | _ =>
415removed let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
416removed `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
417removed | Tm.app _ _ => do
418removed let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
419removed let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
420removed `(stlcTm| $f $a)
421removed | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
422removed let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
423removed let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
424removed let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
425removed `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
426removed | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
427removed let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
428removed let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
429removed let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
430removed `(stlcTm| if $c then $t else $e)
431removed | _ => do
432removed -- `subst` is defined below, so it is matched by name rather than with
433removed -- `match_expr`; a substitution prints in its own bracket notation.
434removed let e ← getExpr
435removed if e.getAppFn.constName? == some `Stlc.subst && e.getAppNumArgs == 3 then
436removed let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
437removed let s ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
438removed let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
439removed `(stlcTm| [$x := $s] $t)
440removed else
441removed match ← delab with
442removed | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTm| $i:ident)
443removed | e => `(stlcTm| ~$e)
444removed (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
445removed
446removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
447removed@[delab app.Stlc.Ty.bool, delab app.Stlc.Ty.arrow]
448removeddef delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
449removed guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
450removed | Ty.bool => true | Ty.arrow _ _ => true | _ => false
451removed match ← delabTyInner with
452removed | `(stlcTy| ~$e) => pure e
453removed | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTy }>)
454removed
455removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
456removed@[delab app.Stlc.Tm.var, delab app.Stlc.Tm.app, delab app.Stlc.Tm.abs,
457removed delab app.Stlc.Tm.tru, delab app.Stlc.Tm.fls, delab app.Stlc.Tm.ite]
458removeddef delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
459removed guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
460removed | Tm.var _ => true | Tm.app _ _ => true | Tm.abs _ _ _ => true
461removed | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true
462removed | _ => false
463removed match ← delabTmInner with
464removed | `(stlcTm| ~($e)) => pure e
465removed | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
466removed | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
467removed
468removed-- Here are the terms we will use as running examples, written in the new
469removed-- notation:
470removed
471removedabbrev idB := <{ λ x : Bool . x }>
472removed
473removedabbrev idBB := <{ λ x : Bool → Bool . x }>
474removed
475removedabbrev idBBBB := <{ λ x : (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) . x }>
476removed
477removedabbrev k := <{ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x }>
478removed
479removedabbrev notB := <{ λ x : Bool . if x then false else true }>
480removed
481removed-- Note that an abstraction `λ x : T . t` (formally, `Tm.abs` applied to `x`,
482removed-- `T`, and `t`) is always annotated with the type `T` of its parameter, in
483removed-- contrast to Lean (and other functional languages like ML, Haskell, etc.),
484removed-- which use type inference to fill in missing annotations. We're not
485removed-- considering type inference at all here.
486removed
487removed-- ## Operational Semantics
488removed
489removed-- To define the small-step semantics of STLC terms, we begin, as always, by
490removed-- defining the set of values. Next, we define the critical notions of *free
491removed-- variables* and *substitution*, which are used in the reduction rule for
492removed-- application expressions. And finally we give the small-step relation
493removed-- itself.
494removed
495removed-- ### Values
496removed
497removed-- To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to consider.
498removed
499removed-- First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation is clear: `true`
500removed-- and `false` are the only values. An `if` expression is never a value.
501removed
502removed-- Second, an application is not a value: it represents a function being
503removed-- invoked on some argument, which clearly still has work left to do.
504removed
505removed-- Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
506removed
507removed-- - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a value — i.e., only
508removed-- if the function's body has been reduced (as much as it can be without
509removed-- knowing what argument it is going to be applied to).
510removed
511removed-- - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter whether `t` is
512removed-- one or not — in other words, we can say that reduction stops at
513removed-- abstractions.
514removed
515removed-- Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes the first choice —
516removed-- for example,
517removed
518removed#reduce fun _x : Bool => 3 + 4
519removed
520removed-- yields:
521removed
522removed-- fun _x => 7
523removed
524removed-- But Lean is rather unusual in this respect. Most functional programming
525removed-- languages make the second choice — reduction of a function's body only
526removed-- begins when the function is actually applied to an argument.
527removed
528removed-- We also make the second choice here.
529removed
530removedinductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
531removed | abs (x : String) (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : Tm.IsValue <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
532removed | tru : Tm.IsValue <{ true }>
533removed | fls : Tm.IsValue <{ false }>
534removed
535removed-- The example terms named above are all abstractions, hence all values. We
536removed-- record that once each, so that the reduction examples can cite the fact by
537removed-- name instead of unfolding the definition again at every use.
538removed
539removedtheorem idB_value : idB.IsValue := .abs ..
540removedtheorem idBB_value : idBB.IsValue := .abs ..
541removedtheorem notB_value : notB.IsValue := .abs ..
542removed
543removed-- Note to developers:
544removed-- The Rocq source follows each inductive definition in this chapter with
545removed-- a `Hint Constructors … : core`, registering the constructors with
546removed-- `auto`; the proofs then lean on `auto`/`eauto` to assemble derivations.
547removed-- We have no counterpart here: the proofs below name their constructors
548removed-- explicitly, in the style of the Types chapter. Lean's `grind` would be
549removed-- the closest analogue if a later pass wants automation.
550removed
551removed-- ### STLC Programs
552removed
553removed-- Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete* program.
554removed
555removed-- Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any undefined
556removed-- variables. We'll see shortly how to define the *free* variables in a STLC
557removed-- term. A complete program, then, is one that is *closed* — that is, that
558removed-- contains no free variables.
559removed
560removed-- (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is often called an
561removed-- *open term*.)
562removed
563removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
564removed-- Is the "shortly" above setting wrong expectations? Where exactly are we
565removed-- defining the free variables in a STLC term? BCP 25: Indeed, we need to
566removed-- define "free"!
567removed
568removed-- Having made the choice not to reduce under abstractions, we don't need to
569removed-- worry about whether variables are values, since we'll always be reducing
570removed-- programs "from the outside in," and that means the `step` relation will
571removed-- always be working with closed terms.
572removed
573removed-- ### Substitution
574removed
575removed-- Now we come to the heart of the STLC: the operation of *substituting* one
576removed-- term for a variable in another term. This operation is used below to define
577removed-- the operational semantics of function application, where we will need to
578removed-- substitute the argument term for the function parameter in the function's
579removed-- body. For example, we reduce
580removed
581removed-- (λx:Bool. if x then true else x) false
582removed
583removed-- to
584removed
585removed-- if false then true else false
586removed
587removed-- by substituting `false` for the parameter `x` in the body of the function.
588removed
589removed-- In general, we need to be able to substitute some given term `s` for
590removed-- occurrences of some variable `x` in another term `t`. Informally, this is
591removed-- written `[x:=s]t` and pronounced "substitute `s` for `x` in `t`."
592removed
593removed-- Here are some examples:
594removed
595removed-- - `[x:=true] (if x then true else false)` yields
596removed-- `if true then true else false`
597removed
598removed-- - `[x:=true] x` yields `true`
599removed
600removed-- - `[x:=true] (if x then x else y)` yields `if true then true else y`
601removed
602removed-- - `[x:=true] y` yields `y`
603removed
604removed-- - `[x:=true] false` yields `false` (vacuous substitution)
605removed
606removed-- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. if y then x else false)` yields
607removed-- `λy:Bool. if y then true else false`
608removed
609removed-- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. x)` yields `λy:Bool. true`
610removed
611removed-- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. y)` yields `λy:Bool. y`
612removed
613removed-- - `[x:=true] (λx:Bool. x)` yields `λx:Bool. x`
614removed
615removed-- The last example is illuminating: substituting `x` with `true` in
616removed-- `λx:Bool. x` does *not* yield `λx:Bool. true`! The reason for this is that
617removed-- the `x` in the body of `λx:Bool. x` is *bound* by the abstraction: it is a
618removed-- new, local name that just happens to be spelled the same as some global
619removed-- name `x`.
620removed
621removed-- Here is the definition, informally...
622removed
623removed-- [x:=s]x = s
624removed-- [x:=s]y = y if x ≠ y
625removed-- [x:=s](λx:T. t) = λx:T. t
626removed-- [x:=s](λy:T. t) = λy:T. [x:=s]t if x ≠ y
627removed-- [x:=s](t₁ t₂) = ([x:=s]t₁) ([x:=s]t₂)
628removed-- [x:=s]true = true
629removed-- [x:=s]false = false
630removed-- [x:=s](if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) =
631removed-- if [x:=s]t₁ then [x:=s]t₂ else [x:=s]t₃
632removed
633removed-- ... and formally:
634removed
635removedsection
636removedset_option hygiene false in
637removedlocal macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
638removed | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
639removed `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
640removed
641removeddef subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm :=
642removed match t with
643removed -- `.var y`, not `<{ ~y }>`: `y` is the variable's *name*, a `String`
644removed -- (see the note below the definition).
645removed | .var y =>
646removed if x = y then s else t
647removed | <{ λ ~y : ~T . ~t₁ }> =>
648removed if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
649removed | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
650removed <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
651removed | <{ true }> =>
652removed <{ true }>
653removed | <{ false }> =>
654removed <{ false }>
655removed | <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
656removed <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>
657removedend
658removed
659removedmacro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
660removed | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
661removed `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
662removed
663removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: substitution
664removed
665removed-- One more line registers substitutions with the printer, so that a goal
666removed-- mentioning one reads as `[x := s] t` rather than as a `subst` application.
667removed
668removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
669removed@[delab app.Stlc.subst]
670removeddef delabSubst : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
671removed match ← delabTmInner with
672removed | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
673removed | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
674removed
675removed-- As we did for the evaluators in the Slang chapter, we pair the definition
676removed-- with one *simplification lemma* per constructor, saying how `subst` behaves
677removed-- on that constructor. The variable and abstraction cases each need two
678removed-- lemmas, since substitution treats a bound name differently depending on
679removed-- whether it is the name being substituted for.
680removed
681removedvariable (x y : String) (s t t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T : Ty)
682removed
683removed@[simp] theorem subst_var_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var x) }> = s := by
684removed simp [subst]
685removed
686removed@[simp] theorem subst_var_ne (h : x ≠ y) : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var y) }> = .var y := by
687removed simp [subst, h]
688removed
689removed@[simp] theorem subst_abs_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~x : ~T . ~t }> := by
690removed simp [subst]
691removed
692removed@[simp] theorem subst_abs_ne (h : x ≠ y) :
693removed <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~y : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t }> := by
694removed simp [subst, h]
695removed
696removed@[simp] theorem subst_app :
697removed <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
698removed
699removed@[simp] theorem subst_tru : <{ [~x := ~s] true }> = <{ true }> := rfl
700removed
701removed@[simp] theorem subst_fls : <{ [~x := ~s] false }> = <{ false }> := rfl
702removed
703removed@[simp] theorem subst_ite :
704removed <{ [~x := ~s] (if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃) }> =
705removed <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }> := rfl
706removed
707removed-- _Quiz:_
708removed
709removed-- What is the result of the following substitution?
710removed
711removed-- [x:=s](λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))
712removed
713removed-- (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
714removed
715removed-- (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
716removed
717removed-- (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
718removed
719removed-- (4) none of the above
720removed
721removed-- *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to define if we consider
722removed-- the case where `s`, the term being substituted for a variable in some other
723removed-- term, may itself contain free variables. We say that `s` is an *open* term.
724removed
725removed-- Here is an example. Using the above definition to substitute the open term
726removed
727removed-- s = λx:Bool. r
728removed
729removed-- (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global resource) for the free
730removed-- variable `z` in the term
731removed
732removed-- t = λr:Bool. z
733removed
734removed-- where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
735removed
736removed-- λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
737removed
738removed-- where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been "captured" by the binder at
739removed-- the beginning of `t`.
740removed
741removed-- Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle that the names of
742removed-- bound variables do not matter. For example, if we rename the bound variable
743removed-- in `t`, e.g., let
744removed
745removed-- t' = λw:Bool. z
746removed
747removed-- then `[z:=s]t'` is
748removed
749removed-- λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
750removed
751removed-- which does not behave the same as the substituting in the original `t`:
752removed
753removed-- [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
754removed
755removed-- That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change how `t` behaves
756removed-- under our simple substitution. So substitution gets more complicated in
757removed-- that setting, but fortunately we don't have that problem in our STLC
758removed-- variant.
759removed
760removed-- Fortunately, since we are only interested here in defining the `step`
761removed-- relation on *closed* terms (i.e., terms like `λx:Bool. x` that include
762removed-- binders for all of the variables they mention), we can sidestep this extra
763removed-- complexity, but it must be dealt with when formalizing richer languages.
764removed
765removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): substi_correct ⭐⭐⭐
766removed
767removed-- The definition that we gave above defines substitution as a *function*.
768removed-- Suppose, instead, we wanted to define substitution as an inductive
769removed-- *relation* `Substi`. We've begun the definition by providing the
770removed-- `inductive` header and one of the constructors; your job is to fill in the
771removed-- rest of the constructors and prove that the relation you've defined
772removed-- coincides with the function given above.
773removed
774removedinductive Substi (s : Tm) (x : String) : Tm → Tm → Prop where
775removed | var1 :
776removed Substi s x (.var x) s
777removed-- FILL IN HERE
778removed
779removedtheorem substi_correct (s : Tm) (x : String) (t t' : Tm) :
780removed <{ [~x := ~s] ~t }> = t' ↔ Substi s x t t' := by
781removed sorry
782removed
783removed-- ### Reduction
784removed
785removed-- The small-step reduction relation for STLC now follows the same pattern as
786removed-- the ones we have seen before. Intuitively, to reduce a function
787removed-- application, we first reduce its left-hand side (the function) until it
788removed-- becomes an abstraction; then we reduce its right-hand side (the argument)
789removed-- until it is also a value; and finally we substitute the argument for the
790removed-- bound variable in the body of the abstraction. This last rule, written
791removed-- informally as
792removed
793removed-- (λx:T. t₁₂) v₂ ⟶ [x:=v₂] t₁₂
794removed
795removed-- is traditionally called *beta-reduction*.
796removed
797removed-- v.IsValue
798removed-- ----------------------- (appAbs)
799removed-- (λx:T. t) v ⟶ [x:=v]t
800removed
801removed-- t₁ ⟶ t₁'
802removed-- ---------------- (app1)
803removed-- t₁ t₂ ⟶ t₁' t₂
804removed
805removed-- v.IsValue
806removed-- t₂ ⟶ t₂'
807removed-- ---------------- (app2)
808removed-- v₁ t₂ ⟶ v₁ t₂'
809removed
810removed-- ... plus the usual rules for conditionals:
811removed
812removed-- -------------------------------- (ifTrue)
813removed-- (if true then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₁
814removed
815removed-- --------------------------------- (ifFalse)
816removed-- (if false then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₂
817removed
818removed-- t₁ ⟶ t₁'
819removed-- ---------------------------------------------------- (ifStep)
820removed-- (if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) ⟶ (if t₁' then t₂ else t₃)
821removed
822removed-- This is *call by value* reduction: to reduce an application `(t₁ t₂)`, we
823removed
824removed-- - first reduce `t₁` to a value: a function `λx:T. t`
825removed
826removed-- - then reduce the argument `t₂` to a value `v`
827removed
828removed-- - then reduce the application itself by substituting `v` for the bound
829removed-- variable `x` in the body `t`.
830removed
831removed-- Formally:
832removed
833removedsection
834removedset_option hygiene false in
835removedlocal notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
836removed
837removedinductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
838removed | appAbs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t v : Tm) (hv : v.IsValue) :
839removed <{ (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) ~v }> ⟶ <{ [~x := ~v] ~t }>
840removed | app1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
841removed <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
842removed | app2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
843removed <{ ~v₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ ~t₂' }>
844removed | ifTrue (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
845removed <{ if true then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₁
846removed | ifFalse (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
847removed <{ if false then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₂
848removed | ifStep (t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
849removed <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
850removedend
851removed
852removedscoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
853removedscoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
854removed
855removed-- As in the Smallstep chapter, `⟶*` is the multi-step closure of `⟶` — that
856removed-- is, `Multi` applied to this chapter's step relation. We inherit its
857removed-- reflexivity lemma along with it, so a zero-step execution goal `t ⟶* t` is
858removed-- closed by `rfl`.
859removed
860removed-- _Quiz:_
861removed
862removed-- What does the following term step to?
863removed

865removed
866removed-- (A) `λx:Bool. x`
867removed
868removed-- (B) `λx:Bool → Bool. x`
869removed
870removed-- (C) `(λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x)`
871removed
872removed-- (D) none of the above
873removed
874removed-- _Quiz:_
875removed
876removed-- What does the following term step to?
877removed
878removed-- (λx:Bool → Bool. x)
879removed-- ((λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x))
880removed-- ⟶ ???
881removed
882removed-- (A) `λx:Bool. x`
883removed
884removed-- (B) `λx:Bool → Bool. x`
885removed
886removed-- (C) `(λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x)`
887removed
888removed-- (D) `(λx:Bool → Bool. x) ((λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x))`
889removed
890removed-- (E) none of the above

926removed-- ### Examples
927removed
928removed-- Example:
929removed
930removed-- (λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x) ⟶* λx:Bool. x
931removed
932removed-- i.e.,
933removed
934removed-- idBB idB ⟶* idB
935removed
936removedexample : <{ ~idBB ~idB }> ⟶* idB := by
937removed apply Multi.step (y := idB)
938removed · exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> idB idB_value
939removed · rfl
940removed
941removed-- Example:
942removed
943removed-- (λx:Bool → Bool. x) ((λx:Bool → Bool. x) (λx:Bool. x))
944removed-- ⟶* λx:Bool. x
945removed
946removed-- i.e.,
947removed
948removed-- (idBB (idBB idB)) ⟶* idB.
949removed
950removedexample : <{ ~idBB (~idBB ~idB) }> ⟶* idB := by
951removed -- the same reduction happens twice, so we name it
952removed have step₁ : <{ ~idBB ~idB }> ⟶ idB := by
953removed exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> idB idB_value
954removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~idBB ~idB }>)
955removed · exact .app2 idBB <{ ~idBB ~idB }> idB idBB_value step₁
956removed apply Multi.step (y := idB)
957removed · exact step₁
958removed · rfl
959removed
960removed-- Example:
961removed
962removed-- (λx:Bool → Bool. x)
963removed-- (λx:Bool. if x then false else true)
964removed-- true
965removed-- ⟶* false
966removed
967removed-- i.e.,
968removed
969removed-- (idBB notB) true ⟶* false.
970removed
971removedexample : <{ ~idBB ~notB true }> ⟶* <{ false }> := by
972removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~notB true }>)
973removed · exact .app1 <{ ~idBB ~notB }> notB <{ true }>
974removed (.appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> notB notB_value)
975removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ if true then false else true }>)
976removed · exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool }> <{ if x then false else true }> <{ true }> .tru
977removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ false }>)
978removed · exact .ifTrue <{ false }> <{ true }>
979removed · rfl
980removed
981removed-- Example:
982removed
983removed-- (λx:Bool → Bool. x)
984removed-- ((λx:Bool. if x then false else true) true)
985removed-- ⟶* false
986removed
987removed-- i.e.,
988removed
989removed-- idBB (notB true) ⟶* false.
990removed
991removed-- (Note that this term doesn't actually typecheck; even so, we can ask how it
992removed-- reduces.)
993removed
994removedexample : <{ ~idBB (~notB true) }> ⟶* <{ false }> := by
995removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~idBB (if true then false else true) }>)
996removed · exact .app2 idBB <{ ~notB true }> <{ if true then false else true }> idBB_value
997removed (.appAbs "x" <{ Bool }> <{ if x then false else true }> <{ true }> .tru)
998removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~idBB false }>)
999removed · exact .app2 idBB <{ if true then false else true }> <{ false }> idBB_value
1000removed (.ifTrue <{ false }> <{ true }>)
1001removed apply Multi.step (y := <{ false }>)
1002removed · exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> <{ false }> .fls
1003removed · rfl
1004removed

1027removed
1028removed-- ## Typing
1029removed
1030removed-- Next we consider the typing relation of the STLC, which is meant to prevent
1031removed-- reduction from getting stuck.
1032removed
1033removed-- For instance, the following two STLC terms are both stuck:
1034removed
1035removed-- `if λx:Bool. x then true else false`
1036removed
1037removed-- Here we branch on a function as though it were a boolean.
1038removed
1039removed-- `true false`
1040removed
1041removed-- Here we apply a boolean as though it were a function.
1042removed
1043removed-- ### Contexts
1044removed
1045removed-- Although we are primarily interested in the binary relation `⊢ t ⦂ T`,
1046removed-- relating a closed term `t` to its type `T`, we need to generalize a bit to
1047removed-- make the definitions work.
1048removed
1049removed-- Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively, we
1050removed-- need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed the
1051removed-- binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be *open*).
1052removed-- While checking that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`, we must remember that `x` has
1053removed-- type `T₁₁`, in order to deal with these free occurrences of `x`. Similarly,
1054removed-- `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and typechecking their bodies
1055removed-- could require looking up the declared types of yet more free variables.
1056removed
1057removed-- To keep track of all this, we add a third element to the relation, a
1058removed-- *typing context* `Γ`, which records the types of the variables that may
1059removed-- occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to types.
1060removed
1061removed-- The new *typing judgment* is written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and informally read as
1062removed-- "term `t` has type `T`, given the types of free variables in `t` as
1063removed-- specified by `Γ`".
1064removed
1065removed-- We'll also write `x ↦ T ; Γ` for "update the partial map `Γ` so that it
1066removed-- maps `x` to `T`," following the notation from the `Typeclasses` chapter.
1067removed
1068removed-- With these refinements, we are ready to give informal and formal
1069removed-- specifications of the typing relation.
1070removed
1071removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
1072removed-- I find the FULL explanation above much better than the TERSE one below,
1073removed-- since the question below seems ill-posed without extra context. Why
1074removed-- would one want to type a term `x y` if we've just said that we will
1075removed-- just look at closed terms as our programs?
1076removed
1077removedabbrev Context := PartialMap String Ty
1078removed
1079removed-- A context is a `PartialMap` from variable names to types — the partial maps
1080removed-- of the `Typeclasses` chapter, which are total maps whose values are
1081removed-- optional, so that `none` at a variable means "not bound here".
1082removed
1083removed-- ### Typing Relation
1084removed
1085removed-- Γ x = T₁
1086removed-- ------------ (var)
1087removed-- Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T₁
1088removed
1089removed-- x ↦ T₂ ; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁
1090removed-- ------------------------- (abs)
1091removed-- Γ ⊢ λx:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1092removed
1093removed-- Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1094removed-- Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂
1095removed-- ------------------ (app)
1096removed-- Γ ⊢ t₁ t₂ ⦂ T₁
1097removed
1098removed-- ----------------- (tru)
1099removed-- Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
1100removed
1101removed-- ------------------ (fls)
1102removed-- Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
1103removed
1104removed-- Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁ Γ ⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁
1105removed-- --------------------------------------------- (ite)
1106removed-- Γ ⊢ if t₁ then t₂ else t₃ ⦂ T₁
1107removed
1108removed-- We can read the three-place relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` as: "under the assumptions
1109removed-- in Γ, the term `t` has the type `T`."
1110removed
1111removed-- In the formal development, we write this judgment inside the same
1112removed-- `<{ .. }>` brackets we use for types and terms, as introduced by the
1113removed-- following notational conventions.
1114removed
1115removed-- A context is written `∅` when empty and `x ↦ T ; Γ` when extended with a
1116removed-- binding, and `~e` escapes to a Lean expression of type `Context`. The whole
1117removed-- judgment then goes inside the same `<{ … }>` brackets as terms, written
1118removed-- with the turnstile and colon of the Types chapter: `<{ Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`.
1119removed
1120removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: contexts and judgments
1121removed
1122removed-- Contexts get a grammar of their own, `stlcCtx`. The **meaning** is the map
1123removed-- update we already have — `x ↦ T ; Γ` expands to exactly the `Typeclasses`
1124removed-- chapter's partial-map update on `Γ` — but its surface syntax has to be our
1125removed-- own, because inside these brackets all three positions are in object
1126removed-- syntax. Writing the map notation directly would mean writing the binding as
1127removed-- `"x" →ₚ <{ Bool → Bool }> ; Γ`: the name quoted, and the type escaped back
1128removed-- out of the brackets it belongs in. The grammar hides those two encoding
1129removed-- details, and nothing else.
1130removed
1131removeddeclare_syntax_cat stlcCtx
1132removedsyntax:max "∅" : stlcCtx
1133removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : stlcCtx
1134removedsyntax:max stlcVar " ↦ " stlcTy " ; " stlcCtx : stlcCtx
1135removed
1136removedsyntax:max (name := judgeBracket) "<{ " stlcCtx " ⊢ " stlcTm " ⦂ " stlcTy " }>" : term
1137removed
1138removedopen Lean in
1139removed/-- The `Context` denoted by a context expression. -/
1140removedpartial def ctxTerm (G : TSyntax `stlcCtx) : MacroM Term :=
1141removed match G with
1142removed | `(stlcCtx| ∅) => `((∅ : Context))
1143removed | `(stlcCtx| ~$e) => pure e
1144removed | `(stlcCtx| $x:stlcVar ↦ $T:stlcTy ; $G:stlcCtx) => do
1145removed `(PartialMap.update $(← ctxTerm G) $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1146removed | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
1147removed
1148removed-- As with `subst`, the judgment notation is used inside the definition it
1149removed-- names, so it is introduced in two steps: the rule below is declared `local`
1150removed-- with hygiene off, so the `HasType` in its expansion resolves to the
1151removed-- relation being declared, and after the `section` closes it is declared
1152removed-- again for real use.
1153removed
1154removedsection
1155removedset_option hygiene false in
1156removedlocal macro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1157removed | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1158removed `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1159removed
1160removedinductive HasType : Context → Tm → Ty → Prop where
1161removed | var (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ : Ty) (h : Γ[x] = some T₁) :
1162removed <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~(Tm.var x) ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1163removed | abs (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm)
1164removed (h : <{ ~x ↦ ~T₂ ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1165removed <{ ~Γ ⊢ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>
1166removed | app (Γ : Context) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
1167removed (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₂ }>) :
1168removed <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1169removed | tru (Γ : Context) :
1170removed <{ ~Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
1171removed | fls (Γ : Context) :
1172removed <{ ~Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
1173removed | ite (Γ : Context) (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T₁ : Ty)
1174removed (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Bool }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>)
1175removed (h₃ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1176removed <{ ~Γ ⊢ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1177removed
1178removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: the judgment, for real
1179removed
1180removed-- Closing the `section` retires the hygiene-free rule; the same rule is then
1181removed-- declared again, hygienically, for every later use.
1182removed
1183removedend
1184removed
1185removedmacro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1186removed | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1187removed `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1188removed
1189removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing judgments back
1190removed
1191removed-- As with terms, a judgment prints back in its own notation, so that a goal
1192removed-- reads as `<{ x ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ x ⦂ Bool }>` rather than as a `HasType` applied
1193removed-- to a chain of map updates.
1194removed
1195removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter in
1196removed/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1197removedcontext prints as `x ↦ Bool ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1198removedpartial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1199removed | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1200removed | `($x:str →ₚ $T) => do
1201removed unexpandCtx (← `($x →ₚ $T ; ∅))
1202removed | `($x:str →ₚ $T ; $G) => do
1203removed let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1204removed let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1205removed if isPlainName x.getString then
1206removed `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1207removed else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1208removed match T with
1209removed | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1210removed | _ => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($T) ; $G')
1211removed | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1212removed
1213removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter in
1214removed@[app_unexpander Stlc.HasType]
1215removeddef HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1216removed | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1217removed do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
1218removed | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $T) =>
1219removed do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1220removed | `($_ $G $t <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1221removed do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $T }>)
1222removed | `($_ $G $t $T) =>
1223removed do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1224removed | _ => throw ()
1225removed
1226removed-- ### Examples
1227removed
1228removedexample : <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . x ⦂ Bool → Bool }> :=
1229removed .abs _ "x" _ _ _ (.var _ "x" _ rfl)
1230removed
1231removed-- The derivation is small enough to write out directly: an abstraction rule
1232removed-- whose premise is the variable rule, and the variable rule's premise — that
1233removed-- the extended context maps `x` to `Bool` — holds by computation, hence
1234removed-- `rfl`.
1235removed
1236removed-- Note to developers:
1237removed-- The Rocq source proves this one, and the next, by `eauto`, having
1238removed-- registered the `has_type` constructors in the `core` hint database; it
1239removed-- also observes that plain `auto` suffices here because the term contains
1240removed-- no application nodes. We have no hint database, so both derivations are
1241removed-- given explicitly.
1242removed
1243removed-- More examples:
1244removed
1245removed-- ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool → Bool. y (y x)
1246removed-- ⦂ Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool.
1247removed
1248removedexample :
1249removed <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . y (y x) ⦂
1250removed Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool }> :=
1251removed .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _
1252removed (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl)
1253removed (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl) (.var _ "x" _ rfl))))
1254removed
1255removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): typing_example_2_full ⭐⭐
1256removed
1257removed-- Prove the same result in tactic mode, applying one rule at a time and
1258removed-- naming the argument type of each application explicitly.
1259removed
1260removedexample :
1261removed <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . y (y x) ⦂
1262removed Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool }> := by
1263removed sorry
1264removed
1265removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): typing_example_3 ⭐⭐
1266removed
1267removed-- Formally prove the following typing derivation holds:
1268removed
1269removed-- ∃ T,
1270removed-- ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool → Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . λ z : Bool .
1271removed-- y (x z)
1272removed-- ⦂ T
1273removed
1274removedexample :
1275removed ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool → Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . λ z : Bool . y (x z)
1276removed ⦂ ~T }> :=
1277removed sorry
1278removed
1279removed-- We can also show that some terms are *not* typable. For example, we can
1280removed-- check that there is no typing derivation assigning a type to the term
1281removed-- `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y` — i.e.,
1282removed
1283removed-- ¬ ∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y ⦂ T
1284removed
1285removedexample : ¬ ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x y ⦂ ~T }> := by
1286removed intro ⟨T, hc⟩
1287removed -- Each `cases` peels off one rule of the derivation, naming the premise it
1288removed -- leaves behind; the context stays small because the old hypothesis goes away.
1289removed cases hc with
1290removed | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
1291removed cases h₁ with
1292removed | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₂ =>
1293removed cases h₂ with
1294removed | app _ _ _ _ _ hf _ =>
1295removed cases hf with
1296removed | var _ _ _ hx =>
1297removed -- `x` is bound to `Bool` in the context, but the application rule
1298removed -- needs it to have an arrow type.
1299removed exact Ty.noConfusion (Option.some.inj hx)
1300removed
1301removed-- Another nonexample:
1302removed
1303removed-- ¬ ∃ S T, ∅ ⊢ λx:S. x x ⦂ T
1304removed
1305removedexample : ¬ ∃ S T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : ~S . x x ⦂ ~T }> := by
1306removed sorry
1307removed
1308removed-- Note to developers:
1309removed-- The Rocq proof gets to the same contradiction through a chain of
1310removed-- `inversion`s and then an induction on the offending type; the `LATER`
1311removed-- note there asks why `eauto 30` makes no progress on the previous
1312removed-- example, and a `NOTATION` note from Ori reports an error with the
1313removed-- associativity of the arrow in one of the inversion hypotheses. Neither
1314removed-- issue arises in this encoding.
1315removed
1316removed-- _Quiz:_
1317removed
1318removed-- Which of the following propositions is *not* provable?
1319removed
1320removed-- (A) `y ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. x ⦂ Bool → Bool`
1321removed
1322removed-- (B) `∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. y x ⦂ T`
1323removed
1324removed-- (C) `∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. x y ⦂ T`
1325removed
1326removed-- (D) `∃ S, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. y x ⦂ (Bool → Bool) → S`
1327removed
1328removed-- _Quiz:_
1329removed
1330removed-- Which of these is not provable?
1331removed
1332removed-- (A) `∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. y x ⦂ T`
1333removed
1334removed-- (B) `∃ S T, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ x x x ⦂ T`
1335removed
1336removed-- (C) `∃ S U T, x ↦ S ; y ↦ U ; ∅ ⊢ λz:Bool. x (y z) ⦂ T`
1337removed
1338removed-- (D) `∃ S T, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool. x (x y) ⦂ T`
1339removed
1340removedend Stlc
