5removedimport TS.SFLCompat
6removed
7removed-- # Types: Type Systems
8removed
9removed-- Note to developers:
10removed-- LATER: For consistency with the STLC definitions in future chapters, it
11removed-- would be better and simpler to represent numbers by a simple nat,
12removed-- rather than as strings of `succ` applied to `0` (which also introduces
13removed-- subtleties that are really not the main point here). But the present
14removed-- formulation is not a big problem either.
15removed--
16removed-- LATER: Harper's lecture from the Milner symposium would make a good
17removed-- support for this lecture.
18removed--
19removed-- LATER: There are a bunch of slides from earlier offerings of CIS500
20removed-- that might be wonderful additions to the TERSE notes.
21removed-- https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1002.pdf
22removed-- https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1004.pdf
23removed
24removed-- Our next major topic is *type systems* — static program analyses that
25removed-- classify expressions according to the "shapes" of their results. We'll
26removed-- begin with a typed version of the simplest imaginable language, to
27removed-- introduce the basic ideas of types and typing rules and the fundamental
28removed-- theorems about type systems: *type preservation* and *progress*. In the
29removed-- next chapter we'll move on to the *simply typed lambda-calculus*, which
30removed-- lives at the core of every modern functional programming language
31removed-- (including Lean!).
32removed
33removed-- ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
34removed
35removed-- To motivate the discussion of type systems, let's begin as usual with a
36removed-- tiny toy language. We want it to have the potential for programs to go
37removed-- wrong because of runtime type errors, so we endow it with two kinds of data
38removed-- — numbers and booleans — where not every operation is defined on both types
39removed-- of data. For example, program terms like `5 + true` and
40removed-- `if 42 then 0 else 1` use undefined operator/data-type combinations.
41removed
42removed-- The language definition is completely routine.
43removed
44removed-- ### Syntax
45removed
46removed-- Here is the syntax of program terms, informally:
47removed
48removed-- t ::= true
49removed-- | false
50removed-- | if t then t else t
51removed-- | 0
52removed-- | succ t
53removed-- | pred t
54removed-- | iszero t
55removed
56removed-- And here it is formally:
57removed
58removednamespace TM
59removed
60removedinductive Tm where
61removed | tru
62removed | fls
63removed | ite (c t e : Tm)
64removed | zero
65removed | succ (t : Tm)
66removed | pred (t : Tm)
67removed | isZero (t : Tm)
68removed
69removed-- #### Notation
70removed
71removed-- Writing terms as raw constructors (`.ite .fls .zero (.succ .zero)`) gets
72removed-- unreadable quickly. We introduce a *concrete syntax* so that a term can be
73removed-- written inside `<{ … }>` — for example `<{ if false then 0 else succ 0 }>`
74removed-- — mirroring the informal grammar above. A bare identifier is spliced as a
75removed-- Lean term (so a variable `t` is written just `t`); `~e` escapes an
76removed-- arbitrary Lean expression, and `( … )` groups.
77removed
78removed-- You do not need to understand exactly how the declarations below work;
79removed-- every object language in this book is given its syntax the same way, so it
80removed-- is worth seeing the pattern once:
81removed
82removed-- - `declare_syntax_cat` adds a new non-terminal to Lean's grammar — here `tm`,
83removed-- the terms of this chapter's language.
84removed
85removed-- - Each `syntax` directive declares one production of that non-terminal, with
86removed-- annotations fixing precedence, and the last one declares the `<{ … }>`
87removed-- brackets that let a `tm` appear where Lean expects a term.
88removed
89removed-- - `macro_rules` then translates the resulting syntax forms into the
90removed-- corresponding constructors of `Tm`.
91removed
92removeddeclare_syntax_cat tm
93removed-- The keyword atoms (`true`/`false`/`succ`/`pred`/`iszero`) are parsed as bare
94removed-- identifiers and dispatched in the macro below, rather than declared as
95removed-- reserved symbols. Reserving them would break ordinary Lean uses of
96removed-- `true`/`false` and clash with the constructor/case names `succ`, `pred`.
97removedsyntax:max num : tm
98removedsyntax:max ident : tm
99removedsyntax:75 ident ppHardSpace tm:76 : tm
100removedsyntax:max "(" tm ")" : tm
101removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : tm
102removedsyntax:50 "if " tm:51 " then " tm:51 " else " tm:51 : tm
103removedsyntax:max "<{ " tm " }>" : term
104removed
105removedopen Lean in
106removedmacro_rules
107removed | `(<{ $n:num }>) =>
108removed if n.getNat == 0 then `(Tm.zero)
109removed else Macro.throwErrorAt n "the only numeric literal in this language is 0"
110removed | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
111removed match x.getId.toString with
112removed | "true" => `(Tm.tru)
113removed | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
114removed | _ => `($x) -- a bare identifier is a spliced Lean term (usually a variable)
115removed | `(<{ $f:ident $e:tm }>) =>
116removed match f.getId.toString with
117removed | "succ" => `(Tm.succ <{ $e }>)
118removed | "pred" => `(Tm.pred <{ $e }>)
119removed | "iszero" => `(Tm.isZero <{ $e }>)
120removed | _ => Macro.throwErrorAt f s!"unknown operator `{f.getId}`"
121removed | `(<{ ($e) }>) => `(<{ $e }>)
122removed | `(<{ ~$e }>) => pure e
123removed | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) => `(Tm.ite <{ $c }> <{ $t }> <{ $e }>)
124removed
125removed-- A *delaborator* closes the loop: it walks a `Tm` value and rebuilds the
126removed-- concrete syntax, so that terms appearing in goals, `#check`, and `#eval`
127removed-- output print as `<{ … }>` rather than as a pile of constructors. (Setting
128removed-- `pp.notation false` turns it off, revealing the raw constructors.) A `Ty`
129removed-- prints as `Bool` or `Nat`.
130removed
131removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing terms back
132removed
133removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
134removed/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `tm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
135removed@[category_parenthesizer tm]
136removeddef tm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
137removed maybeParenthesize `tm true wrapParens prec <|
138removed parenthesizeCategoryCore `tm prec
139removedwhere
140removed wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
141removed let pstx ← `(tm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
142removed return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
143removed
144removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
145removed/-- Rebuild `tm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` term. -/
146removedpartial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `tm) := do
147removed let stx ←
148removed match_expr ← getExpr with
149removed | Tm.tru => `(tm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
150removed | Tm.fls => `(tm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
151removed | Tm.zero => `(tm| 0)
152removed | Tm.succ _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
153removed | Tm.pred _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
154removed | Tm.isZero _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `iszero):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
155removed | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
156removed let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
157removed let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
158removed let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
159removed `(tm| if $c then $t else $e)
160removed | _ => do
161removed -- A bare variable prints without the `~` escape; anything else keeps it.
162removed match ← delab with
163removed | `($i:ident) => `(tm| $i:ident)
164removed | e => `(tm| ~$e)
165removed (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
166removed
167removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
168removed-- The keys are the constants' full names: `Tm` lives in namespace `TM`, and the
169removed-- `delab` attribute does not resolve its argument against the current namespace.
170removed@[delab app.TM.Tm.tru, delab app.TM.Tm.fls, delab app.TM.Tm.zero, delab app.TM.Tm.succ,
171removed delab app.TM.Tm.pred, delab app.TM.Tm.isZero, delab app.TM.Tm.ite]
172removedpartial def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
173removed guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
174removed | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.zero => true
175removed | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true | Tm.isZero _ => true
176removed | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true | _ => false
177removed match ← delabTmInner with
178removed | `(tm| ~$e) => pure e
179removed | e => `(<{ $e }>)
180removed
181removed-- #### Values
182removed
183removed-- *Values* are `true`, `false`, and numeric values (`0`, and `succ` of a
184removed-- numeric value).
185removed
186removedinductive Tm.IsBValue : Tm → Prop where
187removed | tru : Tm.IsBValue <{ true }>
188removed | fls : Tm.IsBValue <{ false }>
189removed
190removedinductive Tm.IsNValue : Tm → Prop where
191removed | zero : Tm.IsNValue <{ 0 }>
192removed | succ (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNValue <{ succ t }>
193removed
194removeddef Tm.IsValue (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsBValue t ∨ Tm.IsNValue t
195removed
196removed-- ### Operational Semantics
197removed
198removed-- Here is the single-step relation, informally.
199removed
200removed-- ----------------------------- (ifTrue)
201removed-- if true then t1 else t2 ⟶ t1
202removed
203removed-- ------------------------------ (ifFalse)
204removed-- if false then t1 else t2 ⟶ t2
205removed
206removed-- t1 ⟶ t1'
207removed-- ----------------------------------------------- (ifStep)
208removed-- if t1 then t2 else t3 ⟶ if t1' then t2 else t3
209removed
210removed-- t1 ⟶ t1'
211removed-- ------------------- (succStep)
212removed-- succ t1 ⟶ succ t1'
213removed
214removed-- ----------- (predZero)
215removed-- pred 0 ⟶ 0
216removed
217removed-- IsNValue v
218removed-- ------------------ (predSucc)
219removed-- pred (succ v) ⟶ v
220removed
221removed-- t1 ⟶ t1'
222removed-- ------------------- (predStep)
223removed-- pred t1 ⟶ pred t1'
224removed
225removed-- ---------------- (isZeroZero)
226removed-- iszero 0 ⟶ true
227removed
228removed-- IsNValue v
229removed-- ------------------------ (isZeroSucc)
230removed-- iszero (succ v) ⟶ false
231removed
232removed-- t1 ⟶ t1'
233removed-- ----------------------- (isZeroStep)
234removed-- iszero t1 ⟶ iszero t1'
235removed
236removed-- The formal rules are below. We are defining them differently than we have
237removed-- previously: We are using the relation's own notation (`⟶`) inside the
238removed-- constructors. We achieve this by defining `Tm.Step` within a `section`, and
239removed-- within that section using `set_option hygiene false` on `⟶` so that the
240removed-- constructors read in this syntax; after the `section` closes, we use a
241removed-- `scoped notation` as we have done before.
242removed
243removedsection
244removedset_option hygiene false in
245removedlocal notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
246removedinductive Tm.Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
247removed | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t1
248removed | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t2
249removed | ifStep (c c' t2 t3 : Tm) (h : c ⟶ c') :
250removed <{ if c then t2 else t3 }> ⟶ <{ if c' then t2 else t3 }>
251removed | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ succ t1 }> ⟶ <{ succ t1' }>
252removed | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⟶ <{ 0 }>
253removed | predSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ pred (succ v) }> ⟶ v
254removed | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ pred t1 }> ⟶ <{ pred t1' }>
255removed | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⟶ <{ true }>
256removed | isZeroSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ iszero (succ v) }> ⟶ <{ false }>
257removed | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ iszero t1 }> ⟶ <{ iszero t1' }>
258removedend
259removed
260removedscoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
261removed
262removed-- The `Tm.IsNValue` premises in `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc` are needed for
263removed-- determinism (this will be proved in an optional exercise below).
264removed
265removed-- Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care about whether the
266removed-- expression being stepped makes global sense — it just checks that the
267removed-- operation in the *next* reduction step is being applied to the right kinds
268removed-- of operands. For example, the term `succ true` cannot take a step, but the
269removed-- almost as obviously nonsensical term
270removed
271removed-- succ (if true then true else true)
272removed
273removed-- can take a step (once, before becoming stuck).
274removed
275removed-- ### Normal Forms and Values
276removed
277removed-- The first interesting thing to notice about this `Tm.Step` relation is that
278removed-- the strong progress theorem from the Smallstep chapter fails here. That is,
279removed-- there are terms that are normal forms (they can't take a step) but not
280removed-- values (they are not included in our definition of possible "results of
281removed-- reduction").
282removed
283removed-- Such terms are *stuck*.
284removed
285removeddef Tm.IsNormalForm (t : Tm) : Prop := _root_.IsNormalForm Tm.Step t
286removed
287removeddef Tm.IsStuck (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsNormalForm t ∧ ¬ Tm.IsValue t
288removed
289removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): some_term_is_stuck ⭐⭐
290removed
291removedtheorem some_term_is_stuck : ∃ t, Tm.IsStuck t := by
292removed sorry
293removed
294removed-- However, although values and normal forms are *not* the same in this
295removed-- language, the set of values is a subset of the set of normal forms.
296removed
297removed-- This is important because it shows we did not accidentally define things so
298removed-- that some value could still take a step.
299removed
300removedtheorem nvalue_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
301removed induction h with
302removed | zero => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
303removed | succ t0 hn0 ih =>
304removed intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
305removed cases hstp with
306removed | succStep _ t1' h => exact ih ⟨t1', h⟩
307removed
308removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): value_is_nf ⭐⭐⭐
309removed
310removed-- (Hint: You will reach a point in this proof where you need to use an
311removed-- induction to reason about a term that is known to be a numeric value. This
312removed-- induction can be performed either over the term itself or over the evidence
313removed-- that it is a numeric value. The proof goes through in either case, but you
314removed-- will find that one way is quite a bit shorter than the other. For the sake
315removed-- of the exercise, try to complete the proof both ways.)
316removed
317removedtheorem value_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
318removed sorry
319removed
320removed-- The "other way" mentioned in the hint proves the same fact by induction on
321removed-- the term itself rather than on the evidence that it is a numeric value. It
322removed-- goes through, but is a bit longer than the `nvalue_is_nf` route above.
323removed
324removedtheorem value_is_nf' : ∀ t, Tm.IsValue t → Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
325removed sorry
326removed
327removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): step_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
328removed
329removed-- Use `value_is_nf` (here, `nvalue_is_nf`) to show that the `Tm.Step`
330removed-- relation is also deterministic.
331removed
332removedtheorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Tm.Step := by
333removed sorry
334removed
335removed-- _Quiz:_
336removed
337removed-- Is the following term stuck?
338removed
339removed-- iszero (if true then (succ 0) else 0)
340removed
341removed-- (A) Yes (B) No
342removed
343removed-- _Quiz:_
344removed
345removed-- What about this one? Is it stuck?
346removed
347removed-- if (succ 0) then true else false
348removed
349removed-- (A) Yes (B) No
350removed
351removed-- _Quiz:_
352removed
353removed-- What about this one? Is it stuck?
354removed
355removed-- succ (succ 0)
356removed
357removed-- (A) Yes (B) No
358removed
359removed-- _Quiz:_
360removed
361removed-- What about this one? Is it stuck?
362removed
363removed-- succ (if true then true else true)
364removed
365removed-- (A) Yes (B) No
366removed
367removed-- (Hint: Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care about whether the
368removed-- expression being stepped makes global sense — it just checks that the
369removed-- operation in the *next* reduction step is being applied to the right kinds
370removed-- of operands.)
371removed
372removed-- *Optional aside, good practice with step relations but tangential to the
373removed-- main development.* We define an alternate step relation `⇢` and a step
374removed-- *function* for it.
375removed
376removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1):
377removed-- `In the Rocq source these were a hidden, never-uncommented draft
378removed-- (with `eval` still to be renamed to `step`). Here they are activated as
379removed-- live Lean. Not sure if we want to keep this.`
380removed
381removed-- Suppose we define an alternate single-step relation, written `t ⇢ t'`, that
382removed-- *drops* the `Tm.IsNValue` premise from the `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc`
383removed-- rules — so `pred (succ t)` and `iszero (succ t)` may step even when `t` is
384removed-- not a numeric value. (It is built with exactly the same notation setup as
385removed-- `Tm.Step`; note `predSucc`/`isZeroSucc` no longer take a premise.)
386removed
387removedsection
388removedset_option hygiene false in
389removedlocal notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
390removedinductive Tm.AltStep : Tm → Tm → Prop where
391removed | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t1
392removed | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t2
393removed | ifStep (t1 t1' t2 t3 : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' →
394removed <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> ⇢ <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
395removed | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ succ t1 }> ⇢ <{ succ t1' }>
396removed | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⇢ <{ 0 }>
397removed | predSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ pred (succ t1) }> ⇢ t1
398removed | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ pred t1 }> ⇢ <{ pred t1' }>
399removed | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⇢ <{ true }>
400removed | isZeroSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ iszero (succ t1) }> ⇢ <{ false }>
401removed | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ iszero t1 }> ⇢ <{ iszero t1' }>
402removedend
403removed
404removedscoped notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
405removed
406removed-- Some questions about this relation (answers inline):
407removed
408removed-- - Is `⇢` deterministic (`∀ t t' t'', t ⇢ t' → t ⇢ t'' → t' = t''`)? No:
409removed-- `pred (succ (pred 0))` steps to both `pred 0` (by `predSucc`) and
410removed-- `pred (succ 0)` (by `predStep`, since `pred 0 ⇢ 0`).
411removed
412removed-- - Is every `Tm.Step` normal form also a `⇢` normal form? No:
413removed-- `pred (succ true)` is stuck for `Tm.Step` but steps under `⇢` (to `true`,
414removed-- by `predSucc`, now that the `Tm.IsNValue` premise is gone).
415removed
416removed-- - Is every `⇢` normal form also a `Tm.Step` normal form? Yes — `Tm.Step` is a
417removed-- subrelation of `⇢`, so anything stuck for `⇢` is stuck for `Tm.Step`.
418removed
419removed-- - Is every value reachable by `Tm.Step` (in many steps) also reachable by `⇢`
420removed-- (in many steps)? Yes, for the same subrelation reason.
421removed
422removed-- - Conversely? No: `iszero (succ true)` reaches the value `false` under `⇢`
423removed-- but is stuck under `Tm.Step`.
424removed
425removed-- A *functional* version computes a single `⇢` step of a term, returning
426removed-- `none` when the term is a `⇢` normal form. This is a nice chance to see a
427removed-- step *function*, which the chapter otherwise gives only as a relation:
428removed
429removeddef alt_simplify_step (t : Tm) : Option Tm :=
430removed match t with
431removed | <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> =>
432removed match alt_simplify_step t1 with
433removed | some t1' => some <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
434removed | none =>
435removed match t1 with
436removed | <{ true }> => some t2
437removed | <{ false }> => some t3
438removed | _ => none
439removed | <{ succ t1 }> =>
440removed match alt_simplify_step t1 with
441removed | some t1' => some <{ succ t1' }>
442removed | none => none
443removed | <{ pred t1 }> =>
444removed match alt_simplify_step t1 with
445removed | some t1' => some <{ pred t1' }>
446removed | none =>
447removed match t1 with
448removed | <{ 0 }> => some <{ 0 }>
449removed | <{ succ t2 }> => some t2
450removed | _ => none
451removed | <{ iszero t1 }> =>
452removed match alt_simplify_step t1 with
453removed | some t1' => some <{ iszero t1' }>
454removed | none =>
455removed match t1 with
456removed | <{ 0 }> => some <{ true }>
457removed | <{ succ t2 }> => some <{ false }>
458removed | _ => none
459removed | _ => none
460removed
461removed-- `pred (succ true)` steps under `⇢` (the dropped `IsNValue` premise) even
462removed-- though it is stuck under `Tm.Step`:
463removedexample : alt_simplify_step <{ pred (succ true) }> = some <{ true }> := rfl
464removedexample : alt_simplify_step <{ if true then 0 else succ 0 }> = some <{ 0 }> := rfl
465removedexample : alt_simplify_step <{ 0 }> = none := rfl
466removed
467removed-- ### Typing
468removed
469removed-- The next critical observation is that, although this language has stuck
470removed-- terms, they are always nonsensical, mixing booleans and numbers in a way
471removed-- that we don't even *want* to have a meaning. We can easily exclude such
472removed-- ill-typed terms by defining a *typing relation* that relates terms to the
473removed-- types (either numeric or boolean) of their final results.
474removed
475removed-- The *typing relation* `⊢ t ⦂ T` relates terms to the types of their
476removed-- results. In informal notation it is often written `⊢ t ⦂ T` and pronounced
477removed-- "`t` has type `T`." The `⊢` symbol is called a "turnstile." The `⦂` between
478removed-- the term and its type is a dedicated type-colon glyph (distinct from an
479removed-- ordinary `:`); in the editor you enter it with the Lean input abbreviation
480removed-- `\tc` followed by a space. Below, we're going to see richer typing
481removed-- relations where one or more additional "context" arguments are written to
482removed-- the left of the turnstile. For the moment, the context is always empty.
483removed
484removed-- ------------- (tru)
485removed-- ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
486removed
487removed-- -------------- (fls)
488removed-- ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
489removed
490removed-- ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool ⊢ t2 ⦂ T ⊢ t3 ⦂ T
491removed-- ----------------------------------- (ite)
492removed-- ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T
493removed
494removed-- --------- (zero)
495removed-- ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat
496removed
497removed-- ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
498removed-- --------------- (succ)
499removed-- ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat
500removed
501removed-- ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
502removed-- --------------- (pred)
503removed-- ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat
504removed
505removed-- ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
506removed-- ------------------ (isZero)
507removed-- ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool
508removed
509removed-- Here are the formal rules.
510removed
511removed-- The typing judgment is written `<{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`: the whole judgment is
512removed-- wrapped in `<{ … }>`, the term is in the object grammar (bare variables, no
513removed-- inner `<{ }>`) and the type as `Bool`/`Nat` (a type variable is spliced,
514removed-- `~T` escapes to a Lean `Ty`). As with `Tm.Step`, we define the relation
515removed-- using its own notation, inside a `section` with `set_option hygiene false`
516removed-- so the bare name `Tm.HasType` in the expansion resolves to the relation
517removed-- being defined; after the `section` we re-declare the same rules
518removed-- hygienically for real use. Unlike `⟶`, the judgment builds on the custom
519removed-- `tm` syntactic category, so it must use `syntax`/`macro_rules` rather than
520removed-- `notation` — which is why it still needs the `app_unexpander` to print the
521removed-- judgment back.
522removed
523removedinductive Ty where
524removed | bool
525removed | nat
526removed
527removedsyntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " ident " }>" : term
528removedsyntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " "~" term:max " }>" : term
529removed
530removedsection
531removedset_option hygiene false in
532removedlocal macro_rules
533removed | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
534removed match T.getId.toString with
535removed | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
536removed | "Nat" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
537removed | _ => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
538removed | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
539removed
540removed-- The actual definition, written in the notation above.
541removedinductive Tm.HasType : Tm → Ty → Prop where
542removed | tru : <{ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
543removed | fls : <{ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
544removed | ite (t1 t2 t3 : Tm) (T : Ty)
545removed (h1 : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool }>) (h2 : <{ ⊢ t2 ⦂ T }>) (h3 : <{ ⊢ t3 ⦂ T }>) :
546removed <{ ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T }>
547removed | zero : <{ ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat }>
548removed | succ (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat }>
549removed | pred (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat }>
550removed | isZero (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool }>
551removedend
552removed
553removed-- The same rules repeated with hygiene enabled, for use after the section.
554removedmacro_rules
555removed | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
556removed match T.getId.toString with
557removed | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
558removed | "Nat" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
559removed | _ => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
560removed | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
561removed
562removed-- Print `Tm.HasType`/`Ty` values back as `<{ ⊢ … ⦂ … }>` notation: `delabTy`
563removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
564removed@[delab app.TM.Ty.bool, delab app.TM.Ty.nat]
565removeddef delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
566removed match_expr ← getExpr with
567removed | Ty.bool => `($(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
568removed | Ty.nat => `($(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
569removed | _ => failure
570removed
571removed@[app_unexpander Tm.HasType]
572removeddef Tm.HasType.unexpand : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
573removed | `($_ <{ $t }> $T:ident) => `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
574removed | `($_ $t:ident $T:ident) => `(<{ ⊢ $(⟨t.raw⟩) ⦂ $T }>)
575removed | `($_ $t $T) => `(<{ ⊢ ~$t ⦂ ~$T }>)
576removed | _ => throw ()
577removed
578removedexample : <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else succ 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
579removed .ite _ _ _ _ .fls .zero (.succ _ .zero)
580removed
581removed-- It's important to realize that the typing relation is a *conservative* (or
582removed-- *static*) approximation: it does not consider what happens when the term is
583removed-- reduced — in particular, it does not calculate the type of its normal form.
584removed
585removedexample : ¬ <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
586removed intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
587removed
588removedexample :
589removed ¬ <{ ⊢ if iszero (succ 0) then succ false else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
590removed intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
591removed
592removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): succ_hastype_nat__hastype_nat ⭐
593removed
594removedexample (t : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ succ t ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }> := by
595removed sorry
596removed
597removed-- ### Canonical forms
598removed
599removed-- The following two lemmas capture the fundamental fact that the definitions
600removed-- of boolean and numeric values agree with the typing relation: a well-typed
601removed-- value of type `Bool` is a boolean value, and of type `Nat` a numeric value.
602removed
603removedtheorem bool_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsBValue t := by
604removed cases hv with
605removed | inl hb => exact hb
606removed | inr hn => cases hn with
607removed | zero => cases hT
608removed | succ t0 h => cases hT
609removed
610removedtheorem nat_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNValue t := by
611removed cases hv with
612removed | inl hb => cases hb <;> cases hT
613removed | inr hn => exact hn

615removed-- ### Progress
616removed
617removed-- The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
618removed
619removed-- The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck — or conversely, if
620removed-- a term is well typed, then either it is a value or it can take at least one
621removed-- step. We call this *progress*.
622removed
623removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_progress ⭐⭐⭐
624removed
625removed-- Complete the formal proof of the `progress` property. (Make sure you
626removed-- understand the parts we've given of the informal proof in the following
627removed-- exercise before starting — this will save you a lot of time.)
628removed
629removedtheorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) : Tm.IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
630removed sorry
631removed
632removed-- _Quiz:_
633removed
634removed-- What is the relation between the *progress* property defined here and the
635removed-- *strong progress* from the Smallstep chapter?
636removed
637removed-- (A) No difference — they mean the same thing
638removed
639removed-- (B) Progress implies strong progress
640removed
641removed-- (C) Strong progress implies progress
642removed
643removed-- (D) No relationship
644removed
645removed-- (E) Dunno
646removed
647removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_progress_informal ⭐⭐⭐
648removed
649removed-- Complete the corresponding informal proof.
650removed
651removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
652removed-- Check the typesetting of this...
653removed
654removed-- *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or else `t ⟶ t'` for
655removed-- some `t'`.
656removed
657removed-- *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
658removed
659removed-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
660removed-- `t = if t1 then t2
661removed-- else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
662removed-- `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step to some
663removed-- `t1'`.
664removed
665removed-- - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and the fact that
666removed-- `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean value (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e.,
667removed-- it is either `true` or `false`. If `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by
668removed-- `ifTrue`, while if `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`.
669removed-- Either way, `t` can step, which is what we wanted to show.
670removed
671removed-- - If `t1` itself can take a step, then, by `ifStep`, so can `t`.
672removed
673removed-- This theorem is more interesting than the strong progress theorem that we
674removed-- saw in the Smallstep chapter, where *all* normal forms were values. Here a
675removed-- term can be stuck, but only if it is ill typed.
676removed
677removed-- _Quiz:_
678removed
679removed-- Quick review: in the language defined at the start of this chapter...
680removed
681removed-- - Every well-typed normal form is a value.
682removed
683removed-- (A) True (B) False
684removed
685removed-- _Quiz:_
686removed
687removed-- In this language...
688removed
689removed-- - Every value is a normal form.
690removed
691removed-- (A) True (B) False
692removed
693removed-- _Quiz:_
694removed
695removed-- In this language...
696removed
697removed-- - The single-step reduction relation is a partial function (i.e., it is
698removed-- deterministic).
699removed
700removed-- (A) True (B) False
701removed
702removed-- _Quiz:_
703removed
704removed-- In this language...
705removed
706removed-- - The single-step reduction relation is a *total* function.
707removed
708removed-- (A) True (B) False

710removed-- ### Type Preservation
711removed
712removed-- The second critical property of typing is that, when a well-typed term
713removed-- takes a step, the result is a well-typed term (of the same type).
714removed
715removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): finish_preservation ⭐⭐
716removed
717removed-- Complete the formal proof of the `preservation` property. (Again, make sure
718removed-- you understand the informal proof fragment in the following exercise
719removed-- first.)
720removed
721removedtheorem preservation (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (he : t ⟶ t') : <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> := by
722removed sorry
723removed
724removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_preservation_informal ⭐⭐⭐
725removed
726removed-- Complete the following informal proof.
727removed
728removed-- *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T` and `t ⟶ t'`, then `⊢ t' ⦂ T`.
729removed
730removed-- *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
731removed
732removed-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
733removed-- `t = if t1 then t2
734removed-- else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
735removed-- `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`.
736removed
737removed-- Inspecting the rules for the small-step reduction relation and remembering
738removed-- that `t` has the form `if ...`, we see that the only ones that could have
739removed-- been used to prove `t ⟶ t'` are `ifTrue`, `ifFalse`, or `ifStep`.
740removed
741removed-- - If the last rule was `ifTrue`, then `t' = t2`. But we know that `⊢ t2 ⦂ T`,
742removed-- so we are done.
743removed
744removed-- - If the last rule was `ifFalse`, then `t' = t3`. But we know that
745removed-- `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
746removed
747removed-- - If the last rule was `ifStep`, then `t' = if t1' then t2 else t3`, where
748removed-- `t1 ⟶ t1'`. We know `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` so, by the IH, `⊢ t1' ⦂
749removed-- Bool`. The
750removed-- `ite` rule then gives us `⊢ if t1' then t2 else t3 ⦂ T`, as required.
751removed
752removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): preservation_alternate_proof ⭐⭐⭐
753removed
754removed-- Now prove the same property again by induction on the *evaluation*
755removed-- derivation instead of on the typing derivation. Begin by carefully reading
756removed-- and thinking about the first few lines of the above proofs to make sure you
757removed-- understand what each one is doing. The set-up for this proof is similar,
758removed-- but not exactly the same.
759removed
760removedtheorem preservation' (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (he : t ⟶ t') : <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> := by
761removed sorry
762removed
763removed-- The preservation theorem is often called *subject reduction*, because it
764removed-- tells us what happens when the "subject" of the typing relation is reduced.
765removed-- This terminology comes from thinking of typing statements as sentences,
766removed-- where the term is the subject and the type is the predicate.
767removed
768removed-- ### Type Soundness
769removed
770removed-- Putting progress and preservation together, we see that a well-typed term
771removed-- can never reach a stuck state.
772removed
773removeddef Tm.MultiStep (t1 t2 : Tm) : Prop := Multi Tm.Step t1 t2
774removed
775removedscoped notation:40 t1:41 " ⟶* " t2:41 => Tm.MultiStep t1 t2
776removed
777removedtheorem soundness (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (hm : t ⟶* t') : ¬ Tm.IsStuck t' := by
778removed induction hm generalizing T with
779removed | refl a =>
780removed intro hst; obtain ⟨hnf, hnv⟩ := hst
781removed cases progress a T hT with
782removed | inl hv => exact hnv hv
783removed | inr hs => exact hnf hs
784removed | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact ih T (preservation a b T hT h1)
785removed

812removed-- ## Additional Exercises
813removed
814removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): subject_expansion ⭐⭐⭐
815removed
816removed-- Having seen the subject reduction property, one might wonder whether the
817removed-- opposite property — subject *expansion* — also holds. That is, is it always
818removed-- the case that, if `t ⟶ t'` and `⊢ t' ⦂ T`, then `⊢ t ⦂ T`? If so, prove it.
819removed-- If not, give a counter-example.
820removed
821removedtheorem subject_expansion :
822removed (∀ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> → <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>)
823removed ∨ ¬ (∀ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> → <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) := by
824removed sorry
825removed
